title: Frontex-supported returns climb in first half of 2026 - European Union
description:
In the first half of the year, 109 Return Specialists were working across 15 Member States.
Around 14 000 people registered for EU reintegration assistance in the first half of 2026, up from around 8 000 a year earlier.
Member States may also enrol other returnees for the EURP as long as they meet the eligibility criteria.
The Commission is expected to propose a further strengthening of Frontex’s mandate on returns, including its support to Member States, in the autumn.
Established in 2004, the Agency’s tasks include monitoring migratory flows, supporting border management, and assisting Member States with return activities.
text:
Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, helped EU Member States return more than 33 000 people to non-EU countries in the first half of 2026, up from around 30 000 in the same period a year earlier. Around two in three of them returned voluntarily.

Some 21 000 people returned voluntarily in the first half of the year, compared with around 19 000 a year earlier. Every return that Frontex supports follows an enforceable return decision, meaning the person has exhausted their legal options to remain in the EU. In a voluntary return, the person complies with that decision and leaves with practical help and, where they qualify, financial support. In a forced return, the decision is enforced because the person has not complied with the obligation to leave. That obligation is the same in both cases.

Whether a return is voluntary or forced is decided by national authorities rather than by Frontex; however, the Agency supports both. Voluntary returns are generally more cost-effective than forced ones, which routinely require escorts, medical and monitoring staff, and in some cases dedicated charter arrangements.

Return Specialists from the Standing Corps talk to people about what returning would involve and what help is available, help national authorities manage cases in the systems used to process returns, and support obtaining from the authorities of countries of origin the identity documents required to travel. In the first half of the year, 109 Return Specialists were working across 15 Member States.

The support does not always stop when the plane lands. Around 14 000 people registered for EU reintegration assistance in the first half of 2026, up from around 8 000 a year earlier. That assistance can mean vocational training, a small grant to start a business, or counselling once someone is back in their country of origin. More than four in five of those who registered had returned voluntarily.*

*Not all the people registered under the EU Reintegration Programme (EURP) were the same people as those returned with Frontex support. Member States may also enrol other returnees for the EURP as long as they meet the eligibility criteria.

The Agency also operationally supports the departures themselves. Frontex Return Escort and Support Officers (FRESOs), also part of the Standing Corps, accompany returnees, help people through airports, and handle the administrative and logistical work behind each flight, including for voluntary returnees who need extra assistance. Over the period, 118 FRESOs were deployed across 11 Member States.

The wider legal framework for returns is also changing. The Regulation establishing a Common European System for Returns, agreed by the European Parliament and the Council in June 2026, sets out common rules for return across the EU, including by making forced return the rule where a person does not cooperate, absconds to another Member State, or poses a security risk. The Commission is expected to propose a further strengthening of Frontex’s mandate on returns, including its support to Member States, in the autumn.

A lower-carbon approach to return flights

With air travel accounting for the large majority of return operations, Frontex has been working to reduce the environmental footprint of its return flights. The Agency prioritises scheduled flights over charter flights whenever this is operationally possible. Under an agreement in place since 2023 with a major European airline, a share of the airline’s revenue from Frontex-funded flights goes towards purchasing Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and other environmental sustainability initiatives, provided that they meet the sustainability criteria set by the International Civil Aviation Organization. In the first half of 2026, this funded the purchase of over 90 tonnes of SAF, mitigating an estimated 313 tonnes of CO2 across the full lifecycle of the fuel, from production to combustion.

Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, supports EU Member States and Schengen-associated Countries in managing the external borders of the European Union. Established in 2004, the Agency’s tasks include monitoring migratory flows, supporting border management, and assisting Member States with return activities. Frontex is building up a Standing Corps of officers who can be deployed to support national authorities on the ground. The Agency is based in Warsaw, Poland.

title: Inside Pittsburgh International Airport's transformation: CEO Christina Cassotis on building ...
authors: International Airport Review, Gabriel Higgins, Aviation Solutions, Copenhagen Optimization, AeroCloud Systems
description:
When Christina Cassotis arrived at Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT) in 2015, many still viewed it through the lens of the hub that it had lost.
The new terminal is viewed by the industry as setting new benchmarks in sustainability, experience and innovation.
International Airport Review Editor, Holly Miles, recently met with the airport CEO to discuss the vision for the terminal and what this means for passengers.
A duty to resilience For Christina’s community, which operates as a major transplant centre, people’s lives literally depend on the airport.
IAR’s Airport Leader of the Year 2026 will be announced at the Airport Honour Awards taking place during the International Airport Summit in Rome on 11 November.
text:
If you missed part 1 of the interview, you can read it here.

When Christina Cassotis arrived at Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT) in 2015, many still viewed it through the lens of the hub that it had lost. A decade later, the airport has pioneered everything from on-site childcare facilities to microgrids to sustainable aviation fuel production and a terminal built for all travellers.

Christina opened the landmark $1.7 billion new terminal on 18 November 2025, the result of more than a decade of planning and four years of construction. The new terminal is viewed by the industry as setting new benchmarks in sustainability, experience and innovation. International Airport Review Editor, Holly Miles, recently met with the airport CEO to discuss the vision for the terminal and what this means for passengers.

An airport built for the local community

Christina said on opening the terminal that it was a “an airport built for Pittsburgh, by Pittsburgh.”

With air travel demand set to double by 2050, the number of travellers with special requirements will increase at Pittsburgh and other airports around the world.

According to Cassotis, the new terminal is designed with accessibility “from the very beginning, from the ground-up” because their mantra is that everyone deserves the right to travel, and they strive to be one of the most accessible airports in the world. It was this goal that saw the airport receive Universal Design Certification from the University at Buffalo’s Centre for Inclusive Design and Environmental Access (IDEA Centre) – the only airport to be awarded this so far.

“We all have an obligation to make physical infrastructure as accessible as possible. We built that into the project from day one, working with groups from across the region and specialists in sustainability, technology, accessibility and other areas.”

In each of the four concourses there are restrooms with universal changing tables, increased seating and rest options, raised crosswalks, accessible height ticketing counters, and improved wayfinding to create a more accessible experience.

The airport also runs a “We Got You” initiative, which is a cross-functional programme designed to assist travellers using people, technology and process. Volunteer ambassadors and customer service staff are equipped with hand-held devices to help passengers more quickly.

For passengers with autism or sensory sensitivities, Presley’s Place is a sensory room located in Concourse A, where they can escape the noisy airport environment and relax.

For mothers, the airport also features two nursing rooms stocked with healthy snacks, bottled water, and words of encouragement from fellow parents written on Post-it notes that adorn the walls as a personal touch.

Recognising that childcare can be a barrier to potential airport employees taking up work and a factor in employees leaving the company, Cassotis took a revolutionary step and opened an on-site childcare facility in September 2023. Providing a childcare option on the same site as an employee’s workplace helps strengthen parents’ work-life balance and supports workforce development – and PIT remains one of the few airports in the world that offer this benefit.

Pittsburgh is one of 325 airports that partner with the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower programme. A discreet lanyard, bracelet, pin or sticker lets airport team members know that the wearer has a hidden disability and may require additional help.

If you are a dog lover, you may be lucky enough to see one of the PIT PAWS – short for pups alleviating worry and stress – the therapy dogs who roam the airport with their ambassador to bring joy (as well as helpful information and tips from the handler) to passengers before their flights.

A duty to resilience

For Christina’s community, which operates as a major transplant centre, people’s lives literally depend on the airport. “People’s lives depend on transplant teams getting in or organs being delivered. If we shut down for a day, it could literally cost somebody their life. I feel that’s a responsibility we all have in this industry: to operate with as much resilience and redundancy as possible.”

This means creating an incredibly resilient airport, which they are doing by linking with manufacturing start-ups, energy developments and tech innovation to ensure that they are fit for multiple different futures and what challenges that would bring.

“We’ve prepared for technologies that we can’t even imagine yet. We made sure fibre runs throughout the terminal, and we’ve ensured that we can expand if required. If a hub operation ever returned, we’re master-planned to add more gates. We also have land available if we need to expand parking or other facilities.”

Having seen other airports such as Los Angeles, Atlanta and Heathrow make headlines due to major power outages, Cassotis decided that this could not happen to them. So, in July 2021, PIT became the first major airport in the world to be entirely powered by on-site natural gas and solar energy through a 23MW microgrid.

“We sit on a large site with access to natural gas, so we developed a microgrid through private sector partners at no cost to the airport. The system produces 23MW of energy while we use around 15MW. Excess power is sold back to the grid. The grid is now our backup rather than our primary power source.”

When the same thing happened to their airport, and fires damaged two of PIT’s substations in March 2025, the microgrid isolated those interconnections, powered the airport independently and prevented any loss of power.

“We’ve saved more than $1 million in utility costs annually, reduced our carbon footprint and created a highly resilient energy system, supported by five natural gas turbines and 10,000 solar panels.”

SAF to take off at PIT

Pittsburgh aims to become the first U.S. airport to produce sustainable aviation fuel on-site and this is something Cassotis believes will drive economic development for both the region and the airport, while helping the airport meet its decarbonisation goals.

“Space and resources prevent some airports from pursuing similar projects, but we hope others will follow. We’re progressing towards development and securing offtake agreements. The project will improve resilience for airlines, while increasing domestic energy production. Our airlines are very supportive of this.”

The airport has pipeline access to the river, which would grant them the opportunity to export fuel by barge or rail, allowing them to supply airports across the U.S. Northeast and Midwest.

The Allegheny County Airport Authority also has ambitions to produce hydrogen on-site which would revolutionise the aviation industry. On-site hydrogen would also be used to power ground vehicles, facilities and fuel cells if realised.

Cassotis is a visionary leader who clearly has her eyes on the future and is laying the groundwork to ensure the airport delivers a fantastic passenger experience and plays a leading role in its community and global aviation for many years to come.

title: Hur Sae-hong charts GS Caltex's path beyond refining - The Korea Herald
description:
Amid sweeping changes in global energy markets, GS Caltex Vice Chair Hur Sae-hong seeks to move South Korea’s energy and chemical company beyond its decades-old focus on refining volumes toward higher-value, lower-carbon businesses.
GS Caltex, Korea’s first private oil refiner, operates the world’s fourth-largest single-site refinery.
“How can we maintain a growth path on a quality basis to ensure we remain sustainable for the future?” Hur said.
His answer is what GS Caltex calls its “Deep Transformation Journey,” built around three pillars of transformation: business, digital and artificial intelligence, and green transformation.
Business transformation, which the company calls BX, seeks to overhaul its mindset, culture and organizational structure.
text:
Amid sweeping changes in global energy markets, GS Caltex Vice Chair Hur Sae-hong seeks to move South Korea’s energy and chemical company beyond its decades-old focus on refining volumes toward higher-value, lower-carbon businesses.

Hur outlined his vision in McKinsey & Co.’s “Leading Asia” interview series and its centennial book, “Shapers & Founders: The Untold Stories of Asia’s Extraordinary Owner-CEOs.” He was featured alongside other Korean business leaders from companies including HD Hyundai and MBK Partners.

A fourth-generation member of GS Group’s founding family, Hur spent more than 18 years working in Japan, the US and Singapore for companies including IBM and Chevron. Those experiences helped shape a management philosophy that combines global adaptability with what he describes as traditional Korean humility.

At its center is “we-dership,” Hur’s term for leadership built collectively. The idea calls on executives to “lead from the top, but move together,” with teamwork underpinning the company’s ambition to remain competitive for the next century.

GS Caltex, Korea’s first private oil refiner, operates the world’s fourth-largest single-site refinery. The company prospered for decades on surging energy demand across Asia, but slowing global growth and the risk of excess supply have challenged its traditional volume-led model.

“How can we maintain a growth path on a quality basis to ensure we remain sustainable for the future?” Hur said.

His answer is what GS Caltex calls its “Deep Transformation Journey,” built around three pillars of transformation: business, digital and artificial intelligence, and green transformation.

Business transformation, which the company calls BX, seeks to overhaul its mindset, culture and organizational structure. Digital and AI transformation, or DAX, focuses on building capabilities internally, including retraining and refining petrochemical engineers through an in-house digital academy.

Green transformation, or GX, seeks to shift the company’s portfolio toward lower-carbon growth areas. These include sustainable aviation fuel, bio-based marine fuel, circular plastics, clean hydrogen, and carbon capture, utilization and storage.

Hur is also pushing for GS Caltex to build what he calls a “black-box advantage” — an internal combination of work processes, organizational capabilities and corporate culture that competitors would struggle to replicate.

Investing in emerging green businesses carries substantial risk, but Hur argues that standing still poses an even greater threat. He describes the status quo as “a killer of sustainable growth.”

To manage that risk, GS Caltex uses marginal abatement cost curves to assess projects according to their cost and emissions-reduction potential, prioritizing lower-risk opportunities.

Hur is also trying to preserve startuplike agility within a large corporation. A newly created "business council" brings senior executives together to lead cross-company strategic projects that might otherwise remain confined within individual business units.

Named one of Stanford Graduate School of Business’ “Centennial Alumni Catalysts” in 2025, Hur said the success of the strategy would ultimately be judged by measurable results.

“For me, sustainability means fundamentally rebalancing our portfolio toward lower-carbon businesses,” he said. “In the end, I believe the only way to demonstrate this commitment is through outcomes, not words.”

title: Innovative Machine Learning Models Advance Soil and Plant Water Tracking
description:
Water typically moves from the land to the atmosphere through soil evaporation and plant transpiration.
However, many existing computer models struggle to distinguish between soil evaporation and plant transpiration.
Researchers developed a hybrid model that provides data-informed estimates of parameters that are difficult to estimate.
Summary Accurately representing evapotranspiration and its partitioning between soil evaporation and plant transpiration is a long-standing challenge in Earth system science.
A multi-institutional team of researchers developed a hybrid evapotranspiration model that integrates machine learning into the Penman–Monteith modeling framework to estimate key surface conductance values while preserving physical constraints.
text:
Water typically moves from the land to the atmosphere through soil evaporation and plant transpiration. This process is called evapotranspiration. It plays a major role in events such as drought and heat waves. However, many existing computer models struggle to distinguish between soil evaporation and plant transpiration.

Researchers developed a hybrid model that provides data-informed estimates of parameters that are difficult to estimate. The model combines a physical framework with machine learning to improve predictions of evapotranspiration and its components across diverse conditions, including heat waves and drought.

The Impact

Understanding and predicting how ecosystems use water is essential to helping communities prepare for heat waves and droughts. A new hybrid model combines a form of artificial intelligence and insights from existing land surface models to create a hybrid model that improves scientists' understanding of Earth system processes. This hybrid approach reveals how environmental factors influence evaporation and transpiration across ecosystems. These factors include radiation, soil moisture, and vegetation. These insights can help scientists improve land surface models in Earth system simulations while highlighting where traditional representations of processes break down and where methods that are physically constrained and data-informed may improve robustness.

Summary

Accurately representing evapotranspiration and its partitioning between soil evaporation and plant transpiration is a long-standing challenge in Earth system science. A multi-institutional team of researchers developed a hybrid evapotranspiration model that integrates machine learning into the Penman–Monteith modeling framework to estimate key surface conductance values while preserving physical constraints. Researchers evaluated the model using observations from 47 National Ecological Observatory Network sites spanning a wide range of environment and vegetation types. The model consistently outperformed traditional physics-based models and purely machine learning approaches, maintained accuracy at new sites, and remained stable under extreme conditions. These results demonstrate a scalable, physically grounded pathway for improving understanding of ecosystem water fluxes.

Funding

This work was primarily supported by the Environmental System Science program within the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science's Biological and Environmental Research program. Support was also received from the Zegar Family Foundation and the National Science Foundation Division of Environmental Biology.

Prof. Dr. Fatma Deniz, President of TU Berlin: “The chemical industry is facing a fundamental transformation. However, many technologies for a climate-neutral and circular-economy-oriented chemical industry have yet to be developed. At TU Berlin, we are combining chemistry and chemical engineering with innovation and entrepreneurship to achieve this. The Chemical Invention Factory – John Warner Center (CIF) will create a space where specialized laboratory infrastructure, scientific expertise, and a strong innovation ecosystem come together. In this way, excellent research will lead to concrete applications and new companies—from Berlin for Europe.”

Dr. Henry Marx, State Secretary for Science and Research: “Berlin is committed to chemistry—and we’re moving forward at a rapid pace. With the Chemical Invention Factory, Berlin is making a targeted investment in a field of research and innovation that is of great importance for industrial value creation, sustainability, and the economic future of our region. In doing so, we are aligning with both the state’s research policy strategy and the federal government’s chemistry agenda. Our goal is clear: excellent research should lead more quickly to new technologies, successful spin-offs, and economic value creation. Berlin has outstanding conditions for this, particularly in the field of chemistry. The Chemical Invention Factory bridges the crucial gap between scientific discovery and startup creation, establishing a hub with nationwide influence. The fact that we are already celebrating the topping-out ceremony less than a year after the groundbreaking demonstrates that Berlin is not only investing in this field of the future—Berlin is moving at full speed.”

Prof. Xaver Egger, managing partner of sehw architektur GmbH: “Innovation arises where people, ideas, and disciplines come together. The CIF combines an open space for interaction with a think tank for research-based innovations that have a societal impact, and unites both under a textile façade to form a shared identity.”

Holger Schöfisch, branch manager at Goldbeck: “For us, innovation doesn’t begin with the use of a building, but rather during the construction process itself. With our systematic construction method, we create the conditions to implement even challenging projects efficiently, in a resource-efficient manner, and to a high standard of quality. Today’s topping-out ceremony demonstrates what is possible when well-thought-out processes, collaborative partnerships, and the commitment of all involved successfully come together.”

From Research Findings to Practical Application

Many innovations in Green Chemistry originate in scientific laboratories. However, on the path to practical application, technology transfer and pre-startup teams often lack the appropriate infrastructure: specialized laboratories and equipment, as well as spaces where new processes can be tested outside the traditional research setting. The Chemical Invention Factory is designed to close precisely this gap.

The new building will provide modern laboratory, analysis, and office spaces for teams developing, among other things, sustainable materials, production methods, and chemical processes. In doing so, the CIF builds on the experience of INKULAB on the Charlottenburg campus. The pilot project featuring chemical lab containers—funded as part of the IHK educational projects—demonstrated early on just how great the need is for specialized infrastructure to facilitate knowledge transfer in chemistry, and how much physical proximity and close collaboration further drive innovative solutions.

As part of the greenCHEM T!Raum initiative, funded by the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space, TU Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, and Humboldt University of Berlin are jointly developing new transfer formats and equipping female students and researchers to make the transition from research to practical application.

This creates a seamless technology transfer chain: from identifying and training scientific talent, through the development of new technology transfer and startup models, to technical validation and scaling in specialized laboratories.

TU Berlin Takes Back Construction Responsibility

The new Chemical Invention Factory building is being constructed by TU Berlin’s construction department, which is acting as the project owner. In May 2025, the university signed the contract with the general contractor Goldbeck, and construction began as early as September of that same year. One year later, the shell of the building is complete—meaning the project remains on schedule and within budget. The design for the new building was created by the Berlin-based architectural firm sehw architektur, which won the design competition.

The CIF is also part of a series of larger construction projects in which TU Berlin is once again taking on responsibility as the project owner. The TULIUM museum and exhibition building is also currently under construction on the main campus, with a topping-out ceremony scheduled for late September. Also in September, another extensive construction project under the university’s responsibility will begin with the renovation of the former civil engineering building, Building B.

title: HKMA Launches Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Phase 2B, Covering Steel and Electric ...
description:
Arthur Yuen, Deputy Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), announced the official launch of the Phase 2B prototype of the Hong Kong Sustainable Finance Taxonomy in conjunction with the opening of Hong Kong Green Week 2026, along with a one-month public consultation.
The market has also launched multiple bonds and loans that meet taxonomy standards, covering sectors such as transportation and energy.
Green Finance Market Performance and Future Plans Hong Kong is a leading green and sustainable bond issuance platform in Asia.
The HKMA previously launched the first phase and Phase 2A of the taxonomy in May 2024 and January of this year, respectively.
The third Hong Kong Green Week is being held this week, attracting over 100 local and international public and private sector organizations, with approximately 60 events scheduled.
text:
Arthur Yuen, Deputy Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), announced the official launch of the Phase 2B prototype of the Hong Kong Sustainable Finance Taxonomy in conjunction with the opening of Hong Kong Green Week 2026, along with a one-month public consultation. The new phase expands the total number of economic activities from 25 to 39, incorporating transition activities such as steel manufacturing, battery recycling, and electric buses for the first time, while also introducing a process-based climate adaptation assessment framework to further strengthen Hong Kong's sustainable finance infrastructure.

In an article published on the HKMA's "InSight" column, Yuen noted that the continuous development and optimization of the taxonomy aims to establish a clear and credible assessment tool for the market, clearly defining which economic activities contribute to green and sustainable development, enabling investment and financing decisions to be evidence-based and facilitating the flow of related capital. He revealed that many banks and corporations have already applied the taxonomy to their investment, financing activities, and sustainable finance frameworks, boosting investor confidence in the "green credentials" of projects.

The funding for Hong Kong's first public hydrogen refueling station came from a green loan certified as compliant with the taxonomy standards. The market has also launched multiple bonds and loans that meet taxonomy standards, covering sectors such as transportation and energy. Kenneth Chan, Executive Director at the HKMA, added that financing models applying the taxonomy include loans and bond issuance, with amounts ranging from tens of millions to billions of Hong Kong dollars, primarily related to energy efficiency and renewable energy projects.

Climate Change Mitigation: 10 New Activities Targeting Hard-to-Abate Sectors

Phase 2B continues to focus on the two major objectives of "mitigation" and "adaptation" to climate change. On the mitigation front, 10 new economic activities have been added across three sectors—transportation, manufacturing, and waste treatment—with three key priorities: supporting critical technologies to drive emissions reduction, providing transition pathways for "hard-to-abate sectors," and facilitating the development of green transportation and low-carbon fuels.

The new phase adds activities including battery manufacturing, battery recycling, and low-carbon technology manufacturing. For steel manufacturing, the authority has established two assessment pathways: one based on "emissions intensity" that recognizes incremental emissions reduction achievements, and another based on "technology improvement" that encourages the adoption of advanced emissions reduction technologies. Companies can select the appropriate assessment approach based on their circumstances, advancing their decarbonization transition within a pragmatic and feasible framework.

On electrification, Phase 2B covers economic activities related to the procurement and use of electric buses, electric minibuses, and electric taxis, supporting the reduction of conventional fuel usage. On low-carbon fuels, the new phase covers the entire Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) value chain, including production, blending, storage, and application, as well as green marine fuels such as the production and application of methanol and ammonia.

Climate Adaptation: First-Ever Process-Based Assessment Approach

Unlike climate "mitigation," climate "adaptation" requires consideration of geographical factors. Even when facing the same risks, different locations may require entirely different response measures. Accordingly, Phase 2B introduces a Process-based Approach (PBA)—a systematic "five-step method" that provides clear guidance on defining project scope, risk identification, measure design and implementation, ongoing monitoring, and continuous improvement.

The PBA retains flexibility to accommodate different scenarios while maintaining rigorous and consistent assessment principles. The approach emphasizes ease of market application: if project proponents have already updated design standards or undertaken other relevant work in response to climate change, certain assessment steps may be simplified or skipped as appropriate to avoid duplicate evaluation.

On climate "adaptation," Phase 2B introduces two categories of measures: "whitelist" and "non-whitelist." Whitelist measures have undergone rigorous assessment and are confirmed to make substantive contributions to climate adaptation. The new phase adds 11 whitelist measures, expanding coverage to the energy, transportation, construction, information and communications technology, and risk management and response sectors.

Non-whitelist measures focus on coastal management and flood management, referencing the Hong Kong SAR Government's guidelines to provide a reference list in the taxonomy, identifying 13 non-whitelist measures and examples of technical indicators used for assessment.

Green Finance Market Performance and Future Plans

Hong Kong is a leading green and sustainable bond issuance platform in Asia. In the first half of this year, green and sustainable bonds issued in Hong Kong totaled $20.2 billion (approximately NT$640 billion), up 3% year-on-year, outperforming the region's flat growth.

Chan expects the Phase 2B taxonomy to be officially launched between the end of this year and early next year, with systematic data collection on bank usage to begin in the second half of next year. The HKMA will further expand the scope of the taxonomy in the future. The HKMA previously launched the first phase and Phase 2A of the taxonomy in May 2024 and January of this year, respectively.

Yuen stated that the HKMA will continue to leverage Green Week to consolidate and enhance Hong Kong's influence as a sustainable finance hub. The authority will also develop practical application guidelines based on market needs, assist the industry in effectively utilizing the taxonomy, and gather insights on banking sector adoption through surveys and other means, providing reference for future discussions on whether to incorporate the taxonomy into banking supervisory policy.

The third Hong Kong Green Week is being held this week, attracting over 100 local and international public and private sector organizations, with approximately 60 events scheduled. The HKMA will continue to be guided by market developments, public policy, industry priorities, and the latest technological advancements in updating the taxonomy, while maintaining communication with market participants and stakeholders to drive the taxonomy's greater role in Hong Kong's sustainable finance ecosystem.

text:
Suara.com - Selama ini, minyak kelapa lebih akrab dengan kebutuhan pangan. Bahan baku nabati ini digunakan untuk berbagai produk, mulai dari minyak goreng, margarin, cokelat, selai, hingga krimer nabati.

Namun, pemanfaatannya berpotensi melampaui kebutuhan di dapur. Minyak kelapa juga dapat diolah menjadi bahan bakar pesawat yang lebih berkelanjutan atau sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

Peluang ini tengah dikembangkan Badan Riset dan Inovasi Nasional (BRIN) melalui penelitian material metal-organic framework (MOF). Teknologi tersebut ditujukan untuk membantu mengubah minyak nabati menjadi hidrokarbon yang dapat digunakan sebagai bahan baku SAF.

Pengembangan ini berangkat dari persoalan besar di sektor penerbangan: ketergantungan terhadap bahan bakar fosil masih tinggi. Selama bahan bakar konvensional masih menjadi sumber energi utama pesawat, upaya mengurangi emisi karbon dari sektor penerbangan menghadapi tantangan besar.

“Pengembangan SAF menjadi salah satu alternatif untuk mendukung transisi energi karena sektor penerbangan masih bergantung pada bahan bakar fosil,” kata peneliti Pusat Riset Kimia Molekuler BRIN, Deliana Dahnum, dalam webinar Jejak Kimia Molekuler (JKM) Edisi ke-11, Jumat (28/8).

Mencari cara mengubah minyak nabati menjadi bahan bakar pesawat

Minyak nabati tidak bisa langsung digunakan sebagai bahan bakar pesawat. Salah satu tahapan pentingnya adalah deoksigenasi, yakni proses menghilangkan kandungan oksigen dari bahan baku untuk menghasilkan hidrokarbon yang sesuai dengan karakteristik bahan bakar penerbangan.

Di sinilah material MOF dikembangkan. Tim peneliti BRIN mencoba merekayasa struktur dan situs aktif material tersebut agar proses konversi minyak nabati dapat berlangsung lebih optimal sekaligus menghasilkan produk yang lebih sesuai untuk kebutuhan bioavtur.

Hasil penelitian menunjukkan penggunaan nikel sebesar 10 persen pada MOF mampu mengonversi minyak kelapa menjadi hidrokarbon hingga 99 persen, dengan selektivitas terhadap bioavtur mencapai 91,6 persen.

Proses tersebut berlangsung selama empat jam, dengan tekanan hidrogen 30 bar dan suhu 350 derajat Celsius.

Angka ini menunjukkan adanya kemajuan dalam upaya meningkatkan selektivitas produk. Namun, capaian di laboratorium juga menunjukkan bahwa teknologi tersebut masih membutuhkan pengembangan sebelum dapat diterapkan dalam skala yang lebih luas.

MOF dibuat agar bisa disesuaikan

Salah satu pendekatan yang digunakan peneliti adalah memanfaatkan ZIF-67, salah satu jenis MOF yang tersusun dari ion kobalt dan ligan 2-metilimidazol. Material ini digunakan sebagai sacrificial template untuk menghadirkan logam aktif, termasuk nikel, yang kemudian berperan dalam proses konversi minyak nabati.

Tim peneliti juga menguji jenis logam lain untuk mengetahui material mana yang paling sesuai dengan jalur reaksi dan karakteristik produk yang dihasilkan.

Pendekatan tersebut penting karena kebutuhan material untuk proses konversi tidak selalu sama. Karakteristik minyak nabati, jalur reaksi, hingga jenis hidrokarbon yang diinginkan dapat memengaruhi material yang diperlukan.

“Kita berupaya memahami interaksi antara logam dan pengikat organik (ligan) di dalam MOF,” ujar Deliana.

Menurut dia, salah satu keunggulan MOF adalah strukturnya dapat dimodifikasi sesuai kebutuhan. Komposisi material dan situs aktifnya juga dapat direkayasa sehingga karakteristik material bisa dikendalikan.

“MOF dapat kita modifikasi sesuai dengan kebutuhan. Struktur dan komposisinya dapat ditentukan, begitu juga situs aktifnya. Dengan demikian, kita dapat mengontrol karakteristik material tersebut,” kata Deliana, dikutip dari laman BRIN, Jumat (4/9).

Dari hasil laboratorium menuju SAF

Pengembangan SAF berbasis minyak nabati menawarkan salah satu alternatif untuk mengurangi ketergantungan penerbangan terhadap bahan bakar fosil. Indonesia memiliki keuntungan berupa ketersediaan beragam bahan baku nabati yang dapat diteliti untuk kebutuhan tersebut.

Tetapi, keberhasilan di laboratorium belum otomatis berarti bahan bakar tersebut siap digunakan secara komersial. Masih diperlukan pengujian lebih lanjut untuk memastikan efisiensi proses, kualitas dan konsistensi bahan bakar, ketersediaan bahan baku, serta kelayakan penerapannya dalam skala industri.

Karena itu, pekerjaan berikutnya bukan sekadar menghasilkan hidrokarbon dari minyak kelapa, melainkan memastikan teknologi tersebut dapat bekerja secara konsisten, efisien, dan memenuhi standar yang dibutuhkan industri penerbangan.

Dengan pendekatan itu, riset MOF tidak hanya menawarkan kemungkinan baru dalam memanfaatkan minyak kelapa. Penelitian ini juga menunjukkan bagaimana bahan baku nabati yang selama ini lebih banyak digunakan untuk pangan dapat dikembangkan menjadi bagian dari pilihan teknologi untuk mendukung transisi energi di sektor penerbangan.

title: Methanol Qualified as a Feedstock for Sustainable Aviation Fuel - chemeurope.com
description:
Throughout the multi-year project, the project partners closely supported the ASTM qualification process as members of the Methanol-to-Jet Task Force.
In this context, the early assessment of fuel quality was a key indicator of the project’s success.
Sustainable Methanol as the Basis for a New Aviation Fuel SAF production based on MTJ technologies uses sustainable methanol derived from biogenic sources or produced from hydrogen and captured CO₂.
“The goal is to produce larger quantities of fuel in order to conduct further research and demonstrations, thereby paving the way for the industrial implementation of methanol-based Sustainable Aviation Fuel,” adds Dr. Franz Mantei, project manager of the SAFari project.
The SAFari project has been funded by the Federal Ministry of Transport (BMV) since December 1, 2022, for a period of six years.
text:
Throughout the multi-year project, the project partners closely supported the ASTM qualification process as members of the Methanol-to-Jet Task Force. The findings from the evaluation process were thus incorporated into the project work at an early stage and taken into account in the development of the production process. In this context, the early assessment of fuel quality was a key indicator of the project’s success. Since only small quantities of fuel were initially available during this development phase, the prescreening method developed at the DLR Institute of Combustion Technology was employed. It enables a comprehensive evaluation of fuel quality even with small sample quantities and provides an early assessment of whether a fuel meets the requirements of the ASTM specification. The results were immediately incorporated into process and catalyst development and helped ensure that the methanol-to-jet (MTJ) blending components developed in the project were specifically tailored to meet the anticipated international specification requirements.

Sustainable Methanol as the Basis for a New Aviation Fuel

SAF production based on MTJ technologies uses sustainable methanol derived from biogenic sources or produced from hydrogen and captured CO₂. In the methanol-to-olefins (MTO) synthesis, this methanol is converted into short- chain olefins, with water—a byproduct—removing the oxygen from the process. The short-chain olefins are then combined in an oligomerization process to form long-chain olefins, resulting in a product mixture that is liquid at room temperature. Through hydrogenation with hydrogen, the olefins are converted into stable paraffins. The result is a fuel blend that meets the aviation industry’s stringent requirements.

“In the SAFari project, we are working with our partners to develop an innovative process that aims to achieve a carbon-based SAF yield of over 85 percent by weight through customized catalysts and in-process recycling of material streams and heat. “With the successful completion of the ASTM qualification process, one of the biggest hurdles for demonstration and scaling has now been overcome,” explains Dr. Elias Frei, Head of the Hydrogen Technologies Division at Fraunhofer ISE. “Following the successful ASTM qualification, the project is now focusing on further optimizing and scaling up the manufacturing process,” says Dr. Achim Schaadt, Head of the Sustainable Synthesis Products Division, looking ahead. “The goal is to produce larger quantities of fuel in order to conduct further research and demonstrations, thereby paving the way for the industrial implementation of methanol-based Sustainable Aviation Fuel,” adds Dr. Franz Mantei, project manager of the SAFari project. The market potential for this technology is enormous: for European air traffic alone, the mandated quotas will result in approximately 40 million metric tons by 2050.

In addition to Fraunhofer ISE, the consortium for the SAFari project (“Sustainable Aviation Fuels based on Advanced Reaction and Process Intensification”) includes ASG Analytik-Service AG, BP Europa SE, Clariant Produkte (Deutschland) GmbH, the German Aerospace Center (DLR) (DLR), Technip Energies France S.A.S., Südzucker AG, the Federal Association of the German Aviation Industry (BDL), and Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH. The consortium thus covers the entire value chain. The SAFari project has been funded by the Federal Ministry of Transport (BMV) since December 1, 2022, for a period of six years.

text:
The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) will start its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) levy for all origin-destination passengers and general and business aviation flights departing Singapore from 1 January 2027, for tickets or services sold from 1 October 2026. The levy must be reflected as a distinct line item in the fare breakdown, as with other taxes and charges.

The move follows CAAS’ announcement of 10 November 2025.

Treatment of SAF environmental attributes

Under the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (Amendment) Act 2025, all SAF levies collected will be channelled to a statutory SAF Fund and used to purchase SAF and related environmental attributes (EAs) and to cover associated administrative costs.

An environmental attribute is the certified emissions saving of the fuel rather than the fuel itself — the difference in lifecycle carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions between a quantity of SAF and the same quantity of conventional jet fuel. Because that value is tracked separately from the physical litres, it can be allocated or sold to an airline or a company that never burns the fuel, and counted against that party’s offsetting obligations or its sustainability reporting to investors, regulators and other stakeholders.

The Singapore Sustainable Aviation Fuel Company Ltd. (SAFCo), a non-profit company limited by guarantee wholly owned by CAAS, will be the designated collection agent and will also procure, manage, account for and allocate SAF and SAF EAs. SAFCo has been working with airlines and industry stakeholders to develop the operational processes and systems needed for levy returns and collection.

SAFCo will aggregate SAF demand arising from the levies collected and from voluntary SAF demand, and procure SAF and associated EAs. The EAs will be managed separately from the physical fuel and allocated to eligible users in a transparent, traceable and verifiable manner, in compliance with sustainability requirements including the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) Eligible Fuels certification standards.

The EAs procured by SAFCo will have two components, covering Scope 1 and Scope 3 emissions. SAFCo will allocate Scope 1 EAs to aircraft operators to support requirements under CORSIA and ICAO’s long-term aspirational goal of net zero carbon emissions for international aviation by 2050. Allocations will be made in proportion to operators’ relative SAF levy contributions, for operators with material volumes above a minimum allocation threshold of 0.01% of total SAF levies collected. That is expected to cover more than 80 passenger aircraft operators.

SAFCo will centrally manage all Scope 3 EAs, as well as any Scope 1 EAs not allocated to aircraft operators. Those EAs will be made available to organisations seeking to reduce emissions associated with business travel and air freight, and proceeds from their sale will be used to purchase more SAF.

First voluntary SAF trial completed

In August 2026, SAFCo, with support from CAAS, completed procurement for its first voluntary SAF trial, validating the operational, commercial and accounting processes for SAF procurement and EA allocation. Nine companies took part: Boston Consulting Group, Changi Airport Group, DBS Bank, GenZero, Google, OCBC, Temasek, and the airlines Singapore Airlines and Scoot.

SAFCo plans to launch a request for proposal for SAF procurement from the SAF Fund by the end of 2026. The procurement will be conducted in a manner that is transparent, competitive and cost-effective, with the first batch of SAF expected to be delivered and uplifted in mid-2027.

Cargo levy deferred by one year

CAAS will defer the SAF levy for air cargo shipments by one year, to apply to services sold from 1 October 2027 for flights departing Singapore from 1 January 2028. Compared with airlines’ passenger operations, cargo operations are more diverse and involve a wider range of stakeholders — airlines, air express companies, freight forwarders, and shippers — and a wider range of commercial arrangements. Taking industry feedback into account, the one-year deferment will allow more time for CAAS to work with industry to develop and implement a robust levy collection mechanism for cargo shipments on departing flights.

“CAAS has worked closely with airlines and other global industry partners to set up a robust regime for SAF levy collection, procurement and environmental attributes management,” said Han Kok Juan, director-general of CAAS. “In doing so, CAAS seeks to lay the foundation for Singapore to serve as a trusted hub for SAF-related economic activities in the region.”

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Arthur Yuen on Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance
description:
In January this year, we published Phase 2A of the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance (Taxonomy).
Deepening decarbonisation impact Phase 2B continues to focus on the two objectives of climate change mitigation and climate change adaptation.
The technical criteria for manufacturing of iron and steel in Phase 2B have been developed with this approach in mind.
Enhancing climate resilience While the measures above address climate mitigation, adaptation to climate change is equally important.
Introducing a five-step assessment for adaptation projects Unlike climate mitigation, climate adaptation must account for location-specific factors.
text:
In January this year, we published Phase 2A of the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance (Taxonomy). Today, with the opening of Hong Kong Green Week 2026, we are releasing the Phase 2B prototype of the Taxonomy for public consultation. This new phase further expands the coverage to incorporate additional green and transition activities, and refines the assessment framework. It echoes the focuses of this year’s Green Week on inclusive transition as well as climate adaptation and resilience, providing participants with a concrete basis for discussion.

Before introducing Phase 2B, let me reiterate that our ongoing development and enhancement of the Taxonomy aims to establish a clear and credible assessment tool for the market. By clearly defining economic activities that contribute to green and sustainable development, the Taxonomy supports informed decision-making and helps scale up relevant capital flows.

As the Taxonomy continues to be enhanced, a growing number of banks and corporates have adopted it in their investment and financing activities and sustainable finance frameworks, strengthening investors’ confidence in the “greenness” of projects. For example, financing for Hong Kong’s first public hydrogen refuelling station was raised through a green loan certified as aligned with the Taxonomy. A number of Taxonomy-aligned bonds and loans have also been launched in the market in sectors such as transportation and energy, reflecting the Taxonomy’s increasingly widespread adoption.

Deepening decarbonisation impact

Phase 2B continues to focus on the two objectives of climate change mitigation and climate change adaptation. On the mitigation side, 10 new economic activities have been added across the transportation, manufacturing, and waste management sectors. The key focus areas can be summarised in three directions:

Supporting key technologies that drive emissions reduction

Advancing the low-carbon transition requires the support of key enabling technologies. These technologies facilitate the wider adoption of other low-carbon solutions, thereby driving broader emissions-reduction outcomes. Phase 2B therefore introduces activities such as battery manufacturing, battery recycling, and the manufacture of low-carbon technologies. Battery energy storage supports the wider uptake of green electricity by storing renewable energy and supply power when generation is intermittent. Battery recycling supports the circular use of resources and complements the sustainable growth of the electric vehicle market. Furthermore, low-carbon technologies cover the manufacture of semiconductors, motors, and transformers. Semiconductors, in particular, are core components of energy-efficient systems, smart grids, and renewable energy installations, helping innovative decarbonisation technologies reach the market more quickly.

Providing transition pathways for “hard-to-abate sectors”

While certain sectors such as the iron and steel industry are essential to the economy, it is difficult for them to achieve significant emissions reduction in the short run due to technological limitations. These industries are generally referred to as “hard-to-abate sectors”. To achieve economy-wide decarbonisation, it is crucial to support these sectors in their progressive transition and direct capital towards lower-carbon technologies and production methods.

The technical criteria for manufacturing of iron and steel in Phase 2B have been developed with this approach in mind. We have set out two assessment pathways: one based on “emissions intensity”, which recognises progressive emissions reduction; and another based on “technological improvement”, which encourages the adoption of advanced emissions-reduction technologies. Companies can choose the pathway best suited to their circumstances and pursue their transition under a pragmatic and feasible framework.

Supporting the development of green transportation and low-carbon fuels

Decarbonising the transport sector centres on vehicle electrification and the shift to lower-carbon fuels. The Taxonomy therefore gives equal emphasis to both. On electrification, Phase 2B covers the purchase and use of electric buses, electric minibuses, and electric taxis, supporting a reduction in the use of conventional fuels. On low-carbon fuels, Phase 2B covers the entire value chain of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) – including its production, blending, storage, and use – as well as the production and use of green marine fuels such as methanol and ammonia. The relevant technical criteria provide clear reference points for companies committed to accelerating their transition.

Enhancing climate resilience

While the measures above address climate mitigation, adaptation to climate change is equally important. In recent years, extreme weather events such as heatwaves in Europe and flooding in Asia have become more frequent, causing energy disruptions, infrastructure damage, and significant economic losses. Climate risks have become tangible financial risks. However, the United Nations Environment Programme estimates that the global adaptation finance gap amounts to hundreds of billions of US dollars. The market needs a clear and reliable assessment methodology to channel capital into projects that can genuinely enhance resilience.

Introducing a five-step assessment for adaptation projects

Unlike climate mitigation, climate adaptation must account for location-specific factors. Even when the same climate risk is faced, the appropriate response may vary significantly across different locations. For example, coastal areas facing flooding risk may need stronger shoreline protection, while densely built-up urban areas may require improved drainage systems. If not designed properly, adaptation measures can even produce counterproductive outcomes — known as maladaptation. For example, a seawall that protects one area but increases flooding risk for neighbouring communities by altering water-flow patterns.

Phase 2B therefore introduces a process-based approach (PBA). Simply put, it is a systematic five-step assessment that provides clear guidance on (1) defining the project scope; (2) identifying climate risks; (3) designing and implementing adaptation measures; (4) ongoing monitoring; and (5) enhancing the measures. The PBA provides flexibility to accommodate different circumstances while maintaining rigorous and consistent assessment principles. It also supports practical market application. Where project proponents have already updated design standards or undertaken other relevant work in response to climate change, certain assessment steps may, depending on the circumstances, be streamlined or omitted to avoid duplication.

Two categories of adaptation measures

Adaptation measures under Phase 2B fall into two broad categories — “whitelist” and “non-whitelist”:

(a) Whitelist measures

Whitelist measures have been rigorously assessed and confirmed to make a substantial contribution to climate adaptation with low maladaptation risk. Backed by an established evidence base, these measures may be adopted directly by market participants and are deemed to meet Taxonomy requirements without further assessment.

Phase 2B adds 11 whitelist measures, expanding coverage to the energy, transportation, buildings, information and communications technology, and risk management and response sectors. Drawing on the HKSAR Government’s research on coastal and flood management, the Taxonomy includes measures such as flood monitoring devices and early warning systems that address Hong Kong’s key climate risks, thereby responding to local needs.

(b) Non-whitelist measures

Not all adaptation measures can be evaluated against a single set of criteria. For some, effectiveness can only be determined through case-specific assessment and careful management of maladaptation risks. These are categorised as “non-whitelist” measures. Project proponents must follow the PBA and apply appropriate technical metrics in their assessments. For example, for drainage improvement projects, proponents should specify quantifiable parameters, such as design flow and drainage capacity, to demonstrate that the measures can effectively address relevant climate risks without transferring those risks elsewhere.

We have focused initially on two areas closely related to Hong Kong’s major climate risks, namely shoreline protection and flood management. With reference to HKSAR Government guidelines1, the Taxonomy provides a reference list of 13 non-whitelist measures together with examples of technical metrics for assessment.

Looking ahead: building capacity and leveraging Green Week to promote market adoption

We are now conducting a public consultation on the Phase 2B prototype and invite stakeholders across different sectors to actively participate and contribute to the refinement of the final version. Leveraging the platform of the third Hong Kong Green Week, we also look forward to in-depth discussions on how the Taxonomy can be used effectively to accelerate Asia’s transition and strengthen climate resilience.

In just three years, Hong Kong Green Week has become a major annual gathering for Asia’s sustainable development community. Against an increasingly complex and volatile global backdrop, it provides a platform for policymakers, business leaders, experts and academics to exchange views and foster collaboration. The 2026 edition has brought together more than 100 local and international public- and private-sector organisations to host around 60 events. It is particularly encouraging to see broader participation by stakeholders from the real economy, as well as those from overseas and the Chinese Mainland. The discussions have also moved beyond concepts towards practice, exploring climate policy and sustainable finance through the lenses of energy security and economic resilience.

Looking ahead, we will continue to leverage Green Week to consolidate and elevate Hong Kong’s position and influence as a sustainable finance hub. In response to market needs, we will develop practical guidance to support the industry’s effective adoption of the Taxonomy. We will also use surveys and other channels to better understand how the banking sector is adopting the Taxonomy. This will inform future consideration of whether the Taxonomy should be incorporated into our banking supervisory policy.

The HKMA will continue to update the Taxonomy, guided by market developments, public policies, industry priorities, and the latest technological advancements. We will maintain ongoing dialogue with market participants and stakeholders, promoting the Taxonomy to play a greater role in Hong Kong’s sustainable finance ecosystem and further consolidating Hong Kong’s position as a sustainable finance hub in the region.

Arthur Yuen

Deputy Chief Executive

Hong Kong Monetary Authority

7 September 2026

title: Government keeping hands off Temasek investment decisions, Shanmugam says
description:
The government will continue to leave individual investment decisions to Temasek and its portfolio companies, including Singapore Airlines (SIA), as debate grows over the carrier’s exposure to Air India.
In a media doorstop on 5 September, Senior Minister K Shanmugam said government or political interference in individual investments could compromise commercial discipline.
“Decisions will become politicised — shaped by political considerations, rather than commercial judgment,” Shanmugam said.
Shanmugam said the airline, rather than Temasek, is the shareholder in Air India, and that any decision to provide further funding lies with the airline.
Shanmugam added that Temasek is accountable to the government for the performance of its overall portfolio, but not for individual investments or decisions made by its portfolio companies.
text:
Political pressure could compromise commercial discipline, the senior minister added.

The government will continue to leave individual investment decisions to Temasek and its portfolio companies, including Singapore Airlines (SIA), as debate grows over the carrier’s exposure to Air India.

In a media doorstop on 5 September, Senior Minister K Shanmugam said government or political interference in individual investments could compromise commercial discipline.

“Decisions will become politicised — shaped by political considerations, rather than commercial judgment,” Shanmugam said. “In the end, Singaporeans will bear the cost.”

His comments came after reports that Air India is seeking fresh equity from its shareholders, including SIA.

Shanmugam said the airline, rather than Temasek, is the shareholder in Air India, and that any decision to provide further funding lies with the airline.

“It is the responsibility of SIA to assess its investments in Air India in relation to the resources it has for the long-term growth and profitability of the company,” he noted.

SIA has more than $10b in cash reserves and over $3b in undrawn credit facilities.

Shanmugam added that Temasek is accountable to the government for the performance of its overall portfolio, but not for individual investments or decisions made by its portfolio companies.

He pointed out political pressure could also make boards and management more cautious about taking investment risks, which could weigh on returns over the medium to long term.

Meanwhile, SIA shareholders and the public can expect the airline to conduct a rigorous assessment before committing further capital and to remain accountable for its decisions.

“We should leave it to SIA to decide what it does with its investments,” he said. “Of course, SIA shareholders, as well as the broader public, have a right to expect that SIA will be accountable and transparent.”

POSCO International is the latest investor to throw its weight behind Townsville aviation biofuels refinery proponent Jet Zero Australia as the company notches up final development approval for the project.

Jet Zero is also celebrating the completion of a $30 million funding round, managed by Barrenjoey, and supported by investors including Qantas and Airbus.

The proceeds will support completion of front-end engineering design (FEED) for Project Ulysses and its progression towards final investment decision and construction.

The company plans to build a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) plant at Cleveland Bay Industrial Park with the capacity to process at least 183 million litres per year of ethanol to SAF and renewable diesel fuels.

“Completing our $30 million funding round, welcoming POSCO International and securing final development approval are defining milestones for Project Ulysses,” Jet Zero Australia chief executive officer Ed Mason said.

“We are particularly pleased to welcome POSCO International as a strategic investor. Their financial strength, global reach and deep understanding of energy markets make them an ideal partner as we progress the project towards construction.

“Some organisations will buy low-carbon liquid fuels. Others will invest in building the industry. We are fortunate to be backed by organisations committed to doing both.”

A POSCO spokesman said Australia had always been a strategic core hub for the group’s traditional energy and mineral businesses, and this investment marked a significant step in transitioning its portfolio towards a decarbonised future.

“By strategically securing essential low-carbon liquid fuels like SAF and renewable diesel, we are expanding our sustainable energy and feedstock distribution capabilities,” he said.

“Using Project Ulysses as an anchor asset, we look forward to co-developing SAF supply chains that will ultimately grow into a vital hub, contributing to the shared energy security of both South Korea and Australia.”

title: Punching above its acreage: how Hong Kong innovation can solve international crises
description:
A recent breakthrough in advanced battery technology developed by Hong Kong researchers underscores a vital structural reality: despite its compact territorial footprint, the city is consistently engineering scalable solutions to planetary challenges.
Far from functioning merely as an international financial conduit, Hong Kong has emerged as a high-velocity incubator resolving critical bottlenecks across decarbonization, climate resilience, and public health.
