Denmark is changing Sustainable Travel through Copenhagen’s visitor reward model, first tested in 2024 and expanded during summer 2025.
The programme’s confirmed scope covers Sustainable Travel, local experiences and responsible destination planning.
Sustainable Travel Gains Support From Wider European Tourism Policies Copenhagen’s reward programme forms part of a broader change in European destination management.
Together, these initiatives show how Sustainable Travel is being connected with technology, public infrastructure, environmental management and resident wellbeing.
What Happens Next for Sustainable Travel Across Europe Europe has combined its former smart tourism capital and green pioneer competitions under the European Capitals of Tourism identity.
text:
Denmark is changing Sustainable Travel through Copenhagen’s visitor reward model, first tested in 2024 and expanded during summer 2025. The initiative offered selected benefits to visitors who cycled, used public transport, arrived by train, stayed longer or joined environmental activities. Official findings recorded higher bicycle rentals and strong participant satisfaction. The development matters because European cities are seeking practical ways to manage tourism without concentrating solely on visitor growth. Travellers can access optional experiences through qualifying actions. However, the programme creates no visa privileges, passport exemptions, border benefits or changes to existing immigration requirements.

Verified Evidence Defines the Real Scope of the Tourism Development

The central story concerns destination management, responsible visitor behaviour and European tourism policy. Transport and seasonality provide important supporting context. Visa and passport matters represent only a small part of the report because no related immigration change has occurred. The percentages below are an editorial assessment based on the amount, relevance and strength of verified evidence. They are not government statistics or measurements of economic impact.

The verified evidence confirms that Copenhagen tested a voluntary tourism incentive and later increased its scale. It also establishes that European authorities are supporting greener, accessible and digitally managed destinations. The evidence does not prove that rewards reduced total citywide emissions, accommodation prices or visitor congestion. It also does not establish changes in international demand. The programme’s confirmed scope covers Sustainable Travel, local experiences and responsible destination planning.

Copenhagen Expanded Its Rewards After a Successful Initial Trial

Copenhagen introduced CopenPay through a four-week pilot during 2024. Visitors could complete approved actions and receive selected cultural or recreational experiences. Qualifying activities included cycling, using public transport, collecting litter and participating in environmental work. Official results showed that bicycle rentals connected with the initiative increased by 29%. Several tonnes of litter were also collected, although the published summary did not provide one consolidated weight. Participant satisfaction reached 98%, showing that visitors were willing to engage with Sustainable Travel through practical actions.

The programme returned between 17 June and 17 August 2025. It was three times larger than the original trial and involved more than 100 participating attractions and experiences. Eligibility expanded to include travellers arriving by train, using electric vehicles, purchasing sustainable aviation fuel or staying for four nights or longer. Available benefits included bicycle rental, guided visits, attraction access, vegetarian meals and wellbeing activities. Bicycle rentals increased by 59% during this edition. Afterwards, 70% of participants said they intended to maintain responsible habits at home, while the satisfaction rate remained at 98%.

Sustainable Travel Gains Support From Wider European Tourism Policies

Copenhagen’s reward programme forms part of a broader change in European destination management. The European tourism transition framework was published on 4 February 2022 after discussions with authorities and tourism stakeholders. It identified 27 action areas supporting environmental improvement, digitalisation and economic resilience. These areas cover governance, transport, energy, workforce skills, data, accessibility and tourism services. The policy does not force cities to adopt identical rewards. It provides a common structure through which destinations can develop measures suited to their pressures and infrastructure.

European tourism competitions have reinforced this direction. Tampere in Finland and Dubrovnik in Croatia received the two European smart tourism titles for 2026. A European jury selected the cities in November 2025, before their title-year programmes began in March 2026. Tampere received recognition for digital services, accessibility, cultural heritage and responsible growth. Dubrovnik gained recognition for addressing intense visitor pressure around its historic centre. Together, these initiatives show how Sustainable Travel is being connected with technology, public infrastructure, environmental management and resident wellbeing.

Official Figures Reveal the Scale of Europes Seasonal Challenge

European tourism remains heavily concentrated during summer. Official accommodation figures show that July and August generated 31.1% of all nights spent in European Union tourist establishments during 2025. August recorded 3.6 times more overnight stays than January. Croatia experienced the strongest concentration, with 54.5% of its annual nights occurring during those two months. Bulgaria recorded 43.4%, while Greece reached 41.6%. Malta had the lowest measured share at 21.9%, followed by Germany at 24% and Finland at 24.1%.

Short-stay accommodation booked through major online platforms generated 951.6 million guest nights across the European Union during 2025. That total was 11.4% higher than in 2024. The platform figure cannot be added directly to conventional accommodation totals because some properties may appear in both reporting systems. Nevertheless, the data illustrates the scale of demand that destinations must manage. Sustainable Travel initiatives, off-season trips and longer stays could distribute demand more evenly, although further evidence is needed before presenting that outcome as proven.

How Tourism Rewards Could Affect Visitors and Local Communities

The immediate benefit for travellers is access to selected discounts, complimentary admission or local experiences. Participating attractions can encourage visitors to reach them by bicycle or public transport. Hotels may also connect longer stays with responsible tourism packages. Local businesses outside established landmark areas could receive additional spending when programmes guide visitors towards less familiar neighbourhoods. However, no official data confirms that the Copenhagen initiative increased overall visitor arrivals, tourism expenditure or hotel occupancy.

Tourism dispersal also creates challenges. Moving visitors beyond heavily visited districts can distribute income, but it may transfer congestion into residential areas. Cycling cannot serve every visitor, making accessible alternatives essential. Rewards also require funding, participating venues and reliable verification systems. Environmental claims need comparable measurements covering transport emissions, energy, water, waste and community attitudes. Awards and certifications may strengthen destination credibility, but they do not prove that every operator follows the same standards. Effective Sustainable Travel therefore depends on transparent evidence rather than promotional claims alone.

Practical Information for Visitors Considering Rewarded Activities

Participation in Copenhagen’s programme remains voluntary. Travellers do not need to change confirmed European travel plans because of these initiatives. Anyone interested in receiving a benefit should verify whether the programme operates during the intended visit. Offers may have limited capacity, fixed dates or individual conditions. An attraction may also require advance booking or evidence of the completed action.

Travellers should consider these practical steps:

Confirm the programme’s current operating dates.

Check which visitor actions qualify for rewards.

Read the proof and redemption requirements.

Determine whether advance booking is necessary.

Confirm whether the offer provides free admission or a discount.

Review opening hours, age limits and accessibility information.

Retain rail tickets, accommodation records and relevant receipts.

Consult official public transport information before travelling.

Check regular passport and visa requirements separately.

Do not assume that participation provides immigration benefits.

No European authority has announced a passport or visa change connected with these programmes. CopenPay does not provide entry permission, priority border processing or exemptions from Schengen rules. Travellers must continue following requirements based on their nationality, destination and intended length of stay. The rewards affect activities within the destination, not permission to enter it.

What Happens Next for Sustainable Travel Across Europe

Europe has combined its former smart tourism capital and green pioneer competitions under the European Capitals of Tourism identity. The rules and prizes remain unchanged. One category covers cities with more than 100,000 residents and assesses sustainability, accessibility, digitalisation, heritage and creativity. The second normally covers destinations with populations between 25,000 and 100,000 and focuses on green-transition practices. Applications for the 2027 awards closed on 12 June 2026. Four shortlisted cities are due to be announced in September, followed by the selection of two winners in November 2026.

title: The Businesses Accelerating the Sustainability Transition
description:
Sustainability LIVE: The London Summit + Awards returns to London on 8–9 September 2026, bringing more than 1,000 sustainability professionals together at the QEII Centre in Westminster.
The two-day hybrid conference is designed to help senior leaders accelerate the sustainability transition by turning climate and ESG ambitions into business action.
Connecting sustainability across business Accelerating the sustainability transition requires action across the organisation rather than within sustainability teams alone.
Sponsors supporting business transformation The event's sponsors and partners bring expertise across the technologies, services and strategies that businesses can use to accelerate their sustainability transition.
Turn insight into sustainability action Sustainability LIVE is designed to give business leaders the opportunity to connect insight with action as organisations face growing pressure to accelerate their sustainability transition.
text:
Sustainability LIVE: The London Summit + Awards returns to London on 8–9 September 2026, bringing more than 1,000 sustainability professionals together at the QEII Centre in Westminster.

The two-day hybrid conference is designed to help senior leaders accelerate the sustainability transition by turning climate and ESG ambitions into business action.

With more than 50 expert speakers, 10 core content themes and four interactive workshops, the programme will explore how organisations can address the challenges slowing progress.

Sessions will examine climate disclosure, circular economy models, innovation and stakeholder engagement, giving attendees practical perspectives to support sustainability strategies.

Bringing together sustainability executives, business leaders and solution providers creates a space to share approaches, identify opportunities and consider how organisations can move from commitments to measurable progress.

Connecting sustainability across business

Accelerating the sustainability transition requires action across the organisation rather than within sustainability teams alone.

Co-located with Procurement & Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit + Awards, the event connects sustainability leaders with procurement and supply chain professionals working on many of the same challenges.

This cross-functional approach can help businesses align climate targets with sourcing, procurement, supplier engagement and operational strategies.

Attendees can explore how sustainability can become part of everyday business decisions, helping organisations identify where changes can deliver environmental and commercial value.

The event also creates opportunities to learn from peers and compare approaches to implementing sustainability programmes at scale.

By bringing different functions together, Sustainability LIVE provides a setting for businesses to consider how collaboration can accelerate progress across their operations and value chains.

Sponsors supporting business transformation

The event's sponsors and partners bring expertise across the technologies, services and strategies that businesses can use to accelerate their sustainability transition.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is working to develop more sustainable cloud infrastructure, focusing on efficiency and reducing environmental impact while helping customers pursue their sustainability goals.

EcoVadis provides sustainability intelligence, ratings, risk and carbon management tools and e-learning, helping businesses assess performance and improve sustainability across their value chains, with more than 150,000 businesses using its solutions across 185 countries.

Experian brings data, analytics and technology capabilities that can help organisations gain deeper insights across sectors including financial services, healthcare, automotive and insurance, supported by a workforce of 25,200 people across 33 countries.

Sedex helps businesses map, assess, identify and mitigate supply chain risks, supporting sustainability and resilience across a community of 90,000 businesses and 104,000 supply chain sites in 35 sectors.

veritree focuses on the restorative economy, providing traceability and impact measurement for nature-based solutions and connecting businesses with verified environmental and social action, with 150 million trees pledged through its platform.

At Sustainability LIVE: The Leadership Summit in London this June, veritree CEO and Co-Founder Derrick Emsley talked about how hard it is to scale reliable nature-based solutions.

"Nature itself is an incredibly hard, challenging place to work," Derrick says.

"It's not as easy as just a checkbox. In a lot of cases, organisations want to invest in nature, but they don't understand how. And what you see a lot is groups looking for either the input — the tree being planted — or the outcome, which may be carbon or biodiversity.

“But connecting those two dots is where a lot of these projects tend to fail. You might fund the tree planting, but you're not funding the actual healthy forest at the end of it. Or you're trying to fund the carbon impact, but you're not actually funding the appropriate inputs and steps in the journey to get there.

“Then five years in, you realise the impact wasn't actually there.

"Nature itself is a long-term investment. It's about connecting the inputs within those projects to the actual tangible outcomes and monitoring that journey through the entire project.

“That, to us, is what makes a high-quality, high-integrity nature-based project."

Datamaran uses AI to provide continuous intelligence on sustainability risks, regulations, stakeholder needs and peer actions, helping corporate leaders anticipate change and identify risks and opportunities.

Neste brings expertise in renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, with renewable production capacity expected to reach 6.8 million tonnes annually in 2027 as it focuses on renewable fuels that can help customers reduce GHG emissions.

Project Management Institute (PMI) supports organisations and project professionals with knowledge, resources and certifications designed to help deliver projects and transformations effectively and responsibly.

Platinum sponsors SGS United Kingdom Ltd, Watershed and Business Stream add further expertise, spanning sustainability assurance, climate and ESG data, decarbonisation, water efficiency and water management.

Together, the sponsor community reflects the different capabilities businesses need to accelerate the transition – from measuring and managing sustainability performance to transforming supply chains, deploying technology, reducing emissions and delivering projects.

Turn insight into sustainability action

Sustainability LIVE is designed to give business leaders the opportunity to connect insight with action as organisations face growing pressure to accelerate their sustainability transition.

title: El proyecto pionero Eco2fly avanza en su planificación para descarbonizar las industrias de ... - ABC
description:
El proyecto contempla la construcción de nuevas instalaciones junto a la planta cementera que Holcim tiene en Villaluenga de la Sagra (Toledo), donde se llevará a cabo la producción de este combustible sintético para aviación.
Ahora la novedad y avance en este interesante proyecto viene dado por el acuerdo alcanzado entre Volotea, la aerolínea de las pequeñas y medianas ciudades europeas, y Eco2fly.
Hay que tener en cuenta que Volotea ya ha avanzado en la incorporación de combustibles sostenibles de aviación en sus operaciones.
En el caso de Eco2fly, el proyecto está diseñado para la creación de una cadena de valor integrada para la producción de eSAF en España.
Eco2fly reúne capacidades industriales, energéticas y logísticas complementarias, gracias a la participación de Holcim, Eco2fly Power y Exolum, para producir en Europa los combustibles que necesita nuestra aviación.
text:
La iniciativa energética está impulsada y desarrollada por Holcim, Eco2fly Power y Exolum, que trabajan conjuntamente en el desarrollo de una solución destinada a contribuir a la reducción de las emisiones de carbono de dos sectores estratégicos como son la industria cementera y la aviación.

El proyecto contempla la construcción de nuevas instalaciones junto a la planta cementera que Holcim tiene en Villaluenga de la Sagra (Toledo), donde se llevará a cabo la producción de este combustible sintético para aviación. La puesta en marcha de estas instalaciones está prevista para 2032.

Tal y como ya informó ABC, se trata de un innovador proyecto de economía circular en CO2 que transformará las emisiones industriales, que son inherentes al proceso de producción de cemento, en combustible sostenible para la aviación, formando una simbiosis entre ambos. Esta energía puede sustituir directamente al queroseno convencional, de origen fósil, sin necesidad de adaptaciones en las aeronaves ni en la infraestructura de abastecimiento, facilitando así la descarbonización inmediata del transporte aéreo.

Con esta iniciativa se prevé capturar alrededor de 700.000 toneladas de CO₂ generadas en la planta de cemento que Holcim tiene en la localidad toledana de Villaluenga de la Sagra, una de las mayores de España, y transformar la mitad de ese CO₂ en combustible e-SAF de calidad aeronáutica, suficiente para cubrir la mayor parte de la demanda de España en 2031, mientras que el CO₂ restante se almacenará de forma permanente en formaciones geológicas. Parte de ese CO2 será combinado con hidrógeno verde, producido a partir de energía renovable, para convertirlo en combustible sostenible de aviación (e-SAF), alcanzando una producción estimada de 100.000 toneladas anuales.

Ahora la novedad y avance en este interesante proyecto viene dado por el acuerdo alcanzado entre Volotea, la aerolínea de las pequeñas y medianas ciudades europeas, y Eco2fly. Se trata de la firma de un memorando de entendimiento (MoU) para explorar el suministro futuro de eSAF y que refuerza el compromiso de las partes con la descarbonización del transporte aéreo, así como con el desarrollo de una cadena de valor europea para combustibles sostenibles.

Según han informado a este periódico las empresas que acometen este proyecto, el acuerdo «contribuye a avanzar en la senda marcada por ReFuelEU Aviation, el reglamento europeo destinado a impulsar el uso de combustibles sostenibles en la aviación y a reducir la huella ambiental del transporte aéreo, y refuerza el compromiso de Volotea de alcanzar las cero emisiones netas en 2050». A este respecto, hay que tener en cuenta que la normativa establece una incorporación progresiva de SAF en los vuelos con origen en aeropuertos de la Unión Europea: un 2% entre 2025 y 2030; un 6% entre 2030 y 2035, incluyendo un 1,2% de eSAF; y hasta un 70% en 2050.

Las promotoras de esta alianza estratégica indican también que «esta iniciativa conjunta contempla un periodo de suministro de eSAF de diez años desde el inicio comercial de la planta de Eco2Fly, previsto para 2032. Los volúmenes previstos se incorporarán de forma progresiva: 6,5 millones de litros en 2032; entre 12 y 19 millones de litros en 2033 y 2034; y 32 millones litros a partir de 2035».

Hay que tener en cuenta que Volotea ya ha avanzado en la incorporación de combustibles sostenibles de aviación en sus operaciones. En 2025, la compañía utilizó más de siete millones de litros de SAF en sus vuelos, lo que representó el 2,02% de su consumo total de combustible, más de tres veces por encima del promedio estimado de la industria aeronáutica para ese año, situado en el 0,6% de la demanda total de combustible jet. Los SAF utilizados por Volotea permiten reducir alrededor de un 90% las emisiones de CO₂ a lo largo de su ciclo de vida en comparación con el combustible jet fósil actual.

El eSAF (electro Sustainable Aviation Fuel) es un combustible sintético producido a partir de hidrógeno renovable y CO₂ que permite reducir más de un 75% las emisiones netas de gases de efecto invernadero respecto al queroseno fósil convencional. A diferencia de

otros combustibles sostenibles de aviación basados en materias primas biogénicas, el eSAF utiliza electricidad renovable, agua y CO₂ como principales insumos, lo que reduce la dependencia de materias primas limitadas o importadas. Esta característica lo convierte en una solución con alto potencial de escalabilidad a largo plazo y en una palanca estratégica para reforzar la autonomía energética europea. Además, puede utilizarse con las aeronaves y la infraestructura de repostaje existentes, facilitando su implantación en el sector.

En el caso de Eco2fly, el proyecto está diseñado para la creación de una cadena de valor integrada para la producción de eSAF en España. Un proceso que se inicia con la captura de CO₂ procedente del proceso de fabricación del cemento, combinándolo con hidrógeno renovable para la producción de eSAF y su logística asociada. El proyecto conecta capacidades industriales, energéticas y logísticas para unir la descarbonización industrial con la del transporte aéreo e impulsar una cadena de valor nacional y europea para combustibles sostenibles.

Gloria Carreras, directora de ESG de Volotea, ha destacado que «el eSAF será imprescindible para alcanzar la descarbonización de la aviación a largo plazo, pero su desarrollo requiere acelerar las inversiones y aumentar la capacidad de producción en Europa. Este acuerdo con Eco2Fly refleja el compromiso de Volotea con el impulso de proyectos estratégicos que contribuyan a garantizar la disponibilidad futura de eSAF y reforzar la autonomía energética europea».

Por su parte, Javier Esteban, director del proyecto ECO2FLY, ha señalado que «la firma de este memorando con una aerolínea como Volotea valida nuestro modelo de producción de eSAF y supone un impulso decisivo para escalar la oferta de combustibles sintéticos en el mercado español y europeo. Eco2fly reúne capacidades industriales, energéticas y logísticas complementarias, gracias a la participación de Holcim, Eco2fly Power y Exolum, para producir en Europa los combustibles que necesita nuestra aviación. Más allá del impacto en reducción de emisiones, este proyecto contribuirá a disminuir la dependencia del queroseno fósil importado y a reforzar la autonomía estratégica y la independencia energética de la Unión Europea, en línea con los objetivos de REPowerEU».

title: CO₂ to Fuels: e‑Methanol, e‑Methane, Synthetic Aviation Fuel and the Hydrogen Constraint
description:
Synthetic aviation fuels CO₂ and hydrogen can be converted into aviation fuels through several pathways: reverse water-gas shift followed by Fischer–Tropsch synthesis; methanol-to-jet conversion; direct catalytic CO₂ hydrogenation routes; and other power-to-liquid configurations.
Technology Routes Real Cases Case 1: Synthetic fuels for aviation The IEA identifies synthetic hydrocarbon fuels made from captured CO₂ and low-carbon hydrogen as one of the limited decarbonisation options for long-distance transport, particularly aviation.
Summary Conclusion CO₂-derived e-methane, e-methanol, and synthetic aviation fuels can play a valuable role in decarbonising sectors that cannot easily move to direct electrification.

title: Biocarburanti, lo studio TEHA-Eni: “Per l'Europa leva di sicurezza energetica e competitività”
description:
I biocarburanti da materie prime rinnovabili possono rappresentare per l’Europa non soltanto uno strumento di decarbonizzazione dei trasporti, ma anche una leva di sicurezza energetica, diversificazione degli approvvigionamenti e tutela della competitività industriale.
Secondo lo studio, le crisi degli ultimi anni hanno evidenziato come la dipendenza da tecnologie, materie prime e capacità produttive possa produrre conseguenze sistemiche e mettere a rischio la sicurezza energetica europea.
In questa prospettiva, i biocarburanti vengono considerati non soltanto una leva per ridurre le emissioni nei trasporti, ma anche uno strumento di diversificazione, sicurezza energetica e politica industriale.
“Una soluzione già disponibile per i trasporti” La sfida indicata dallo studio è conciliare la transizione energetica con la competitività industriale e con la sostenibilità economica e sociale.
I biocarburanti vengono quindi presentati come una soluzione complementare agli altri vettori energetici, in grado di rafforzare contemporaneamente sicurezza energetica e competitività industriale europea.
text:
I biocarburanti da materie prime rinnovabili possono rappresentare per l’Europa non soltanto uno strumento di decarbonizzazione dei trasporti, ma anche una leva di sicurezza energetica, diversificazione degli approvvigionamenti e tutela della competitività industriale. È il messaggio al centro dello studio realizzato da TEHA Group insieme a Eni e presentato nell’ambito del Forum di Cernobbio organizzato da TEHA.

Uno scenario energetico profondamente cambiato

Il punto di partenza dell’analisi è il mutamento dello scenario energetico globale rispetto alla fase in cui è stato concepito il Green Deal. Secondo lo studio, le crisi degli ultimi anni hanno evidenziato come la dipendenza da tecnologie, materie prime e capacità produttive possa produrre conseguenze sistemiche e mettere a rischio la sicurezza energetica europea. In questo quadro, biocarburanti come HVO, Hydrogenated Vegetable Oil, e SAF, Sustainable Aviation Fuel, vengono indicati come soluzioni già disponibili per diversificare le fonti di approvvigionamento, ridurre le emissioni di gas serra lungo la filiera e, allo stesso tempo, preservare capacità produttive e competenze industriali in Europa.

“Evitare di sostituire una dipendenza con un’altra”

Per Valerio De Molli, managing partner e Ceo di TEHA Group, l’Europa deve evitare che il percorso di transizione energetica si traduca semplicemente nel passaggio da una dipendenza a un’altra. “Una transizione che sostituisce una dipendenza con un’altra non rafforza il continente, ne trasferisce soltanto la vulnerabilità”, ha sottolineato De Molli. In questa prospettiva, i biocarburanti vengono considerati non soltanto una leva per ridurre le emissioni nei trasporti, ma anche uno strumento di diversificazione, sicurezza energetica e politica industriale.

Secondo De Molli, occorre quindi superare un approccio prevalentemente regolatorio e adottare una visione più pragmatica e industriale, capace di tenere conto anche dei nuovi rischi geopolitici.

“Una soluzione già disponibile per i trasporti”

La sfida indicata dallo studio è conciliare la transizione energetica con la competitività industriale e con la sostenibilità economica e sociale. In questo contesto, Stefano Ballista, Ceo di Enilive, ha evidenziato il carattere immediatamente disponibile dei biocarburanti. Questi combustibili, secondo Ballista, possono contribuire a ridurre le emissioni del settore dei trasporti lungo l’intera filiera, sono ampiamente disponibili, possono essere distribuiti attraverso le infrastrutture esistenti e risultano utilizzabili in gran parte delle motorizzazioni diesel attualmente in circolazione.

I biocarburanti vengono quindi presentati come una soluzione complementare agli altri vettori energetici, in grado di rafforzare contemporaneamente sicurezza energetica e competitività industriale europea.

Innovazione e riconversione industriale

L’esperienza maturata da Eni viene richiamata anche come esempio del ruolo che innovazione tecnologica, competenze industriali e professionalità possono avere nei processi di trasformazione. Secondo Ballista, la combinazione di questi fattori può contribuire a generare valore, occupazione e sviluppo sostenibile, sostenendo allo stesso tempo la capacità competitiva dell’Europa.

Le proposte ai policy maker europei

Lo studio formula infine una serie di proposte rivolte ai decisori europei, con l’obiettivo di passare da un’impostazione prevalentemente restrittiva a un approccio giudicato più pragmatico. Uno dei punti centrali riguarda il metodo di misurazione delle emissioni. Secondo l’analisi, l’Europa dovrebbe superare una valutazione concentrata soltanto sulle emissioni allo scarico e prendere invece in considerazione le emissioni generate lungo l’intera filiera, così da riconoscere anche il contributo immediato dei biocarburanti alla riduzione dei gas serra.

Sostenere tecnologie già mature e scalabili

Un altro indirizzo proposto riguarda le tecnologie da sostenere nel percorso di transizione. Lo studio sottolinea come il cambiamento non possa essere affidato esclusivamente a soluzioni destinate a raggiungere la piena maturità nel lungo periodo. L’indicazione è quindi quella di valorizzare anche tecnologie già disponibili, scalabili e capaci di produrre risultati misurabili. Parallelamente, viene evidenziata la necessità di trasformare la base industriale europea, sostenendo la conversione degli impianti esistenti in bioraffinerie e preservando capacità produttive, competenze professionali e occupazione.

Tracciabilità e dati reali per misurare la sostenibilità

L’ultima proposta riguarda la verifica della sostenibilità dei biocarburanti. Il documento indica la necessità di basare le valutazioni su dati reali, facendo ricorso a misurazioni sul campo, sistemi di tracciabilità e tecnologie digitali. L’obiettivo è riconoscere le produzioni realmente addizionali e quelle caratterizzate dai livelli di sostenibilità più elevati, inserendo così i biocarburanti in una strategia europea che tenga insieme decarbonizzazione, sicurezza degli approvvigionamenti e difesa della base industriale.

title: Rolls-Royce Estimates Airlines Could Save Up to $10 Million Annually with New Airbus A350 Engine
description:
Rolls-Royce Projects Significant Fuel Savings with Upgraded Airbus A350 Engine Rolls-Royce has announced that its latest enhancements to the Trent XWB-84 EP engine, which powers the Airbus A350, could enable airlines operating fleets of 20 aircraft to save up to $10 million annually in fuel costs.
The engine manufacturer revealed these projections during a roundtable event ahead of the Farnborough Airshow, emphasizing the improved thrust-specific fuel consumption (SFC) achieved through recent upgrades.
For airlines with larger A350 fleets, these efficiencies could translate into substantial cost reductions amid ongoing volatility in jet fuel prices.
Renowned for its industry-leading fuel efficiency and reliability, the engine has been selected by 90% of profitable airlines operating the A350.
Notably, the Trent XWB-84 EP is capable of operating with up to 50% sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with a long-term goal of achieving 100% SAF compatibility.
text:
Rolls-Royce Projects Significant Fuel Savings with Upgraded Airbus A350 Engine

Rolls-Royce has announced that its latest enhancements to the Trent XWB-84 EP engine, which powers the Airbus A350, could enable airlines operating fleets of 20 aircraft to save up to $10 million annually in fuel costs. The engine manufacturer revealed these projections during a roundtable event ahead of the Farnborough Airshow, emphasizing the improved thrust-specific fuel consumption (SFC) achieved through recent upgrades.

Initially targeting a 1% improvement in SFC, Rolls-Royce now reports gains of up to 1.8%. Rob Watson, President of Civil Aerospace at Rolls-Royce, explained that a 1% improvement in SFC corresponds to nearly $500,000 in annual fuel savings per aircraft. For airlines with larger A350 fleets, these efficiencies could translate into substantial cost reductions amid ongoing volatility in jet fuel prices.

Engine Performance and Environmental Impact

The Trent XWB-84 EP entered service last year with Delta Air Lines as the launch customer and has since accumulated over 100,000 operational hours. Renowned for its industry-leading fuel efficiency and reliability, the engine has been selected by 90% of profitable airlines operating the A350. Notably, the Trent XWB-84 EP is capable of operating with up to 50% sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with a long-term goal of achieving 100% SAF compatibility. This capability positions the engine as a forward-looking option for carriers seeking to reduce carbon emissions and environmental impact.

Industry Challenges and Market Dynamics

Despite these advancements, some challenges persist for airlines considering the new engine. Emirates has expressed concerns regarding long-term engine durability, while United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby has highlighted ongoing engine shortages that could complicate fleet planning and operations. These issues illustrate the complexities airlines face when integrating new technology, even as they aim to benefit from fuel savings and environmental improvements.

Market response to the enhanced Trent XWB-84 EP has been largely positive, with growing interest in the Airbus A350-900 as carriers pursue fleet modernization and cost reduction strategies. However, competition remains intense. General Electric continues to dominate the Boeing 787 market, influencing airline and manufacturer decisions on engine selection and potentially shaping future developments within the widebody aircraft segment.

Investment and Certification

Rolls-Royce’s $1.33 billion (£1 billion) investment in the Trent XWB-84 EP program underscores its commitment to continuous innovation. The engine received certification from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) in December 2024, following extensive redevelopment and thousands of hours of rigorous ground and flight testing. These improvements not only enhance fuel efficiency and reduce emissions but also contribute to quieter and more reliable operations for airlines worldwide.

As the aviation industry confronts increasing pressure to enhance sustainability and manage operational costs, advancements in engine technology such as those embodied by the Trent XWB-84 EP will be pivotal in shaping the future of long-haul air travel.

title: Japan Airlines–Korean Air Strategic Partnership Deepens as Japan Flights Could Surge to ...
description:
Japan Airlines has taken an undisclosed stake in Hanjin KAL, the holding company of Korean Air.
Japan flights are expected to increase from approximately 250 to almost 400 flights per week.
Japan Airlines Makes a Strategic Move Japan Airlines has quietly entered the shareholder structure behind one of Asia’s most important airline groups.
400 Weekly Japan Flights Change The Map The most consequential operational development concerns flight frequency.
The most visible passenger-focused change will be the increase in Japan flights from 250 to 400 flights per week.
text:
Japan Airlines has taken an undisclosed stake in Hanjin KAL, the holding company of Korean Air. The transaction was made concurrently with a significant Japan Airlines-Korean Air strategic partnership announced in Tokyo. The alliance aims to broaden codeshare and frequent flyer partnerships, cargo and ground services. It will evaluate collaborative aircraft maintenance and the removal of sustainable aviation fuel. The largest customer-facing change will occur in December. Korean Air aims to complete its unification with Asiana Airlines at this time. Japan flights are expected to increase from approximately 250 to almost 400 flights per week. This represents an approximate 60% increase. For passengers, the alliance is likely to change connectivity between Japan and South Korea.

Japan Airlines Makes a Strategic Move

Japan Airlines has quietly entered the shareholder structure behind one of Asia’s most important airline groups. The carrier confirmed its acquisition of Hanjin KAL shares on 3 September. However, JAL has not disclosed the investment value or stake size.

No regulatory filing has emerged showing that JAL owns 5 per cent or more. That threshold is significant because Korean disclosure rules require major holdings to be reported. The available evidence therefore does not establish JAL as a substantial shareholder. It confirms an investment, but not its precise influence.

JAL described the move as an independent investment decision. It cited Hanjin KAL’s long-term market value rather than announcing a control objective. That distinction matters. Market observers have nevertheless linked the investment to Hanjin KAL’s increasingly contested ownership structure.

The timing is particularly striking. JAL’s investment arrived as it and Korean Air unveiled a partnership extending well beyond conventional codesharing. The two airlines intend to deepen cooperation across passenger services, cargo, airport operations and future aviation technologies.

For the travel industry, this creates two stories at once. One concerns corporate governance. The other concerns the practical transformation of Korea-Japan air connectivity.

The second story is more immediately relevant to passengers.

400 Weekly Japan Flights Change The Map

The most consequential operational development concerns flight frequency. Korean Air currently operates about 250 weekly flights on Japan routes. Following the integration of Asiana Airlines, that figure is expected to reach approximately 400 flights per week.

That is an additional 150 weekly flights. On a simple annualised basis, the increase represents about 7,800 additional flight movements each year if the stated weekly schedule is maintained.

The increase is tied to Korean Air’s absorption of Asiana Airlines. Korean Air’s formal merger date is scheduled for 16 December 2026, according to its merger notice.

For passengers, frequency can be as important as route launches. More flights can provide greater flexibility around business meetings, weekend breaks and connecting itineraries.

The impact could be especially noticeable on major Korea-Japan city pairs. Seoul, Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya, Fukuoka and Busan are central to the existing network.

However, travellers should not assume that every additional flight will appear as a new nonstop route. Some capacity will come from the integration of existing Asiana services. The actual schedule will depend on fleet planning, airport slots and regulatory approvals.

A Partnership Beyond Airline Alliances

The deal is unusual because Korean Air and JAL belong to different global airline alliances. Korean Air is part of SkyTeam. JAL belongs to oneworld.

Their new relationship therefore sits outside the traditional global alliance framework. It creates a bilateral strategic partnership between two major national carriers.

That distinction has practical importance. Global airline alliances typically provide broad benefits across many member airlines. A bilateral partnership can instead concentrate heavily on a specific geographic market.

Here, the geographic focus is obvious. Japan and South Korea form one of Asia’s most important short-haul aviation markets.

JAL and Korean Air have worked together for decades. Their codeshare relationship began in 2004. Their commercial ties therefore predate today’s broader strategic agreement by more than two decades.

The relationship itself stretches even further back. The airlines trace their cooperation to 1963. Routes between the two countries subsequently expanded, helping support commercial and cultural exchanges.

That long history gives the latest agreement a different character. It is not an entirely new alliance. Instead, it represents a substantial expansion of an established relationship.

What Changes for Travellers?

For travellers, codesharing remains one of the most important elements. Under a codeshare, an airline can market a partner’s operated flight under its own flight number.

That can simplify booking and itinerary construction. It can also make connecting journeys easier when airlines coordinate schedules and ticketing.

The expanded partnership will also cover mileage cooperation. Existing arrangements already allow members to earn or redeem benefits across parts of the two networks. JAL and Korean Air introduced reciprocal mileage cooperation in 2016.

The expanded arrangement could therefore make frequent-flyer planning more useful for travellers moving between the two countries.

The key word remains potential. The airlines have announced the direction of cooperation. Individual fare rules, mileage earning rates, lounge access and booking conditions may vary.

Travellers should therefore check the operating carrier and fare conditions before purchasing tickets.

Korea-Japan Aviation Demand Remains Strong

The expansion comes against a wider Asian aviation backdrop. Japan’s transport ministry reported that the country’s 2026 summer international schedule included 5,445.5 passenger flights per week at the start of the season.

Across passenger and cargo services, the figure reached 5,996.5 weekly flights. Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism also reported increases in passenger services to several Asian markets, including South Korea.

That matters because airline capacity does not expand in isolation. Carriers respond to passenger demand, aircraft availability and airport capacity.

Incheon International Airport also recorded a major milestone in 2025. Passenger traffic reached 74.07 million, according to the airport operator. That surpassed its previous 2019 record by 4.1 per cent.

The airport attributed the record partly to stronger demand on Chinese and Japanese routes. Aircraft movements also reached approximately 425,760 during the year.

These figures provide useful context for the Korean Air-JAL announcement. The partnership arrives while regional aviation is rebuilding and expanding around strong international demand.

The Asiana Merger Is The Catalyst

The December integration of Asiana is central to the new arrangement. Korean Air has formally decided to absorb Asiana Airlines through a small-scale merger structure.

The official merger notice gives 16 December 2026 as the merger date. Korean Air will remain the surviving company. Asiana Airlines will cease to exist as a separate corporate entity following the transaction.

For Japan, the implications are particularly significant.

Asiana has historically operated its own network between South Korea and Japan. Bringing those services into Korean Air’s structure can increase the scale of Korean Air’s Japan network.

JAL will consequently gain access to a larger pool of Korean Air-operated services for potential codeshare cooperation.

The airlines have said the expanded arrangement will include flights connected with the post-merger Japan network. This explains why the expected increase from 250 to 400 weekly flights is central to the partnership.

For travellers, the merger could therefore matter more than the equity investment itself.

Hanjin KAL Faces A Shareholder Test

The investment also carries a corporate dimension that should not be overlooked. Hanjin KAL’s shareholder structure has become increasingly competitive during 2026.

Hanjin Group Chairman Walter Cho and related parties held approximately 20.57 per cent. Hoban Group subsequently increased its holding to 20.15 per cent in July.

Korean exchange disclosures confirm that Hoban raised its holding from 18.46 per cent to 20.15 per cent. The filing described the investment purpose as simple investment.

The resulting gap between the two sides became exceptionally narrow.

Current market data places the Cho-related holding at 20.57 per cent. It also places Hoban’s latest holding at about 19.99 per cent on a later basis, illustrating why shareholder percentages can shift with subsequent transactions.

JAL has not publicly characterised its holding as support for any shareholder group. Consequently, describing it definitively as a “white knight” would go beyond the confirmed facts.

The more defensible reading is that JAL has combined a strategic commercial agreement with a financial investment in its Korean partner’s parent company.

Delta Already Set A Strategic Precedent

JAL is not the first global airline partner to own Hanjin KAL shares. Delta Air Lines holds approximately 14.9 per cent.

That investment became part of a much broader relationship between Delta and Korean Air. The precedent helps explain why the JAL investment has attracted attention.

Strategic airline shareholders can have interests extending beyond financial returns. They can also deepen commercial relationships, support network coordination and align long-term corporate interests.

Still, JAL’s position should not be treated as identical to Delta’s. The size of the JAL holding remains undisclosed.

That uncertainty is important for investors and industry analysts. The next significant question is whether JAL increases its position or leaves the investment unchanged.

Cargo And Airport Operations Move Forward

Passenger connectivity is only one part of the agreement. Korean Air and JAL also intend to expand their cargo relationship.

The airlines are examining joint use of cargo terminals. That could broaden their sales networks while potentially improving the utilisation of expensive airport infrastructure.

They are also considering cooperation in ground handling. Airport labour shortages have become a structural challenge for airlines worldwide.

The partnership includes plans for personnel exchanges and shared cabin-crew training facilities. These measures may appear operational rather than glamorous, but they can have significant long-term value.

Ground operations influence punctuality, turnaround times and airport efficiency. Training cooperation can also reduce duplicated infrastructure and encourage common operating practices.

The proposed cargo cooperation could similarly create benefits beyond passenger travel. Japan and South Korea are major trading economies with extensive regional supply chains.

SAF Cooperation Signals A Longer Horizon

The partnership also looks beyond immediate network expansion. The airlines intend to explore sustainable aviation fuel, commonly known as SAF.

They will consider joint procurement and other cooperation around future aviation technologies. Aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul is another proposed area.

A dedicated task force will examine potential new businesses. The airlines have also indicated interest in startup investment and urban air mobility.

These initiatives demonstrate that the agreement is broader than a conventional codeshare deal.

However, these projects remain exploratory. Travellers should not interpret the announcement as an immediate change to aircraft technology or fuel use.

Instead, it signals where the carriers expect future cooperation to develop.

What Travellers Should Watch Next

The next major milestone will be Korean Air’s December integration with Asiana. That event should clarify how the combined Japan network will operate.

Travellers should watch for changes to flight numbers, operating carriers, timetables and aircraft types. They should also monitor mileage rules once the expanded partnership becomes operational.

The practical checklist is straightforward.

The broader lesson is equally important. A codeshare does not automatically mean identical benefits across every ticket.

Travellers should therefore verify the fare conditions attached to their specific booking.

Why This Matters Across Asian Aviation

The JAL-Korean Air agreement reflects a wider shift in Asian aviation strategy. Airlines are increasingly combining network partnerships with deeper commercial cooperation.

The traditional distinction between airline alliances, joint ventures and bilateral partnerships is becoming less rigid.

This is partly a response to changing passenger flows. It is also a response to rising infrastructure costs and the need to use aircraft more efficiently.

The Korea-Japan market offers a particularly strong environment for such cooperation. Both countries have sophisticated aviation infrastructure. Their major cities also sit within a highly connected regional travel corridor.

For tourism, the implications could extend beyond Seoul and Tokyo. Increased connectivity can support secondary-city travel, short breaks and multi-destination itineraries.

That could benefit destinations across Japan and South Korea if airlines distribute capacity beyond their largest hubs.

A Larger Network With Bigger Ambitions

Japan Airlines’ participation in Hanjin KAL is beyond an insignificant business deal. It is a partnership that can significantly improve air travel between South Korea and Japan.

The most visible passenger-focused change will be the increase in Japan flights from 250 to 400 flights per week. The change will give passengers more flight options as Korean Air will integrate Asiana Airlines in December this year.

The partnership extends beyond ticketing to cover ground handling, cargo, training, MRO (Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul), and SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuel). This provides a more integrated partnership.

JAL’s investment creates a financial connection to a significant regional ally, and Korean Air strengthens business relationships with a large Japanese airline that is not a part of its SkyTeam alliance.

The investment for JAL and Korean Air, as well as passengers, should provide more flight options.

The primary focus after will be how well the partnership makes travel more convenient during the integration in December. This will show how the partnership will provide travel options both within South Korea and Japan.

title: Labor Day Pain at the Pump across the U.S. The Top 10 Most Expensive Gas States vs. the ...
description:
Americans heading out for Labor Day weekend are paying the highest holiday-weekend gasoline prices on record.
AAA’s national regular average closed Friday at $4.1474 a gallon — the first Labor Day ever above $4, and about 95 cents above last year’s $3.20.
The statutory tax line Federal (both states): 18.4¢/gal gasoline · 24.4¢/gal diesel.
The $2.12 California–Texas gap is taxes, carbon programs, a boutique fuel spec, and a refining island.
Have a safe and happy Labor Day Weekend from Pecos Energy.
text:
Americans heading out for Labor Day weekend are paying the highest holiday-weekend gasoline prices on record. AAA’s national regular average closed Friday at $4.1474 a gallon — the first Labor Day ever above $4, and about 95 cents above last year’s $3.20. Diesel is worse: AAA printed an all-time national high of $5.85 a gallon, up roughly $2.14 from a year ago.

The crude backdrop is the same for every state. WTI has been hovering near $90 a barrel on Strait of Hormuz volatility. What is not the same is what each state layers on top of that barrel: excise taxes, sales taxes, carbon programs, boutique fuel specs, and the simple fact that the West Coast refining system is an island. That is why California is at $5.81 while Indiana is at $3.45 — a $2.36-a-gallon spread on the same holiday weekend.

GasBuddy, which compiles station-level reports rather than AAA’s statewide averages, ran a few cents cheaper in late August (national regular near $4.01 on August 31) but told the same story: West Coast isolation at the top, Gulf Coast and Midwest at the bottom, and Patrick De Haan warning that any post-holiday relief depends on crude and the shift to winter-blend gasoline.

Share

Jet fuel: the third pump America rarely talks about

Retail gasoline and on-highway diesel are only two of the three refined products that move the country this weekend.FBO retail Jet-A (what general aviation and many regional operators actually pay at the airport) averaged $7.88 a gallon nationally as of September 4, 2026, per GlobalAir’s survey of more than 3,200 FBOs. 100LL avgas averaged $7.54; sustainable aviation fuel, where it is sold, averaged $10.09. The FAA Alaska region was the most expensive Jet-A market at $9.39; the Central region was cheapest at $7.23.

Wholesale Gulf Coast jet (EIA kerosene-type spot) was about $4.19 a gallon on September 1 — more than double year-ago levels — which is the price airlines hedge against before rack, into-plane, and airport fees.

Federal tax on commercial jet fuel used in domestic commercial aviation is generally 4.4¢/gal; other jet uses can face 21.9¢/gal. California still layers a 2.0¢ state jet excise plus sales-tax prepayment on aircraft jet fuel. Texas taxes aviation fuel at the same 20¢ state rate as motor gasoline.

High jet prices this weekend do not show up on the highway sign, but they show up in airfares, air-cargo rates, and the cost of flying parts, produce, and people over Labor Day.

Diesel: a different ranking, same West Coast problem

Diesel’s national average of $5.85 is a record. California diesel at $7.71 is in a league of its own — $2.25 above Texas and $2.33 above the cheapest state, Oklahoma.’

Most expensive diesel: California $7.71 · Hawaii $7.00 · Washington $6.81 · Nevada $6.17 · Oregon $6.17 · Pennsylvania $6.08 · Alaska $6.01 · Arizona $5.97 · Maryland $5.95 · D.C. $5.90Most affordable diesel: Oklahoma $5.38 · Kansas $5.43 · South Dakota $5.44 · Missouri $5.45 · Texas $5.46 · Louisiana $5.47 · Mississippi $5.50 · Arkansas $5.51 · Kentucky $5.53 · North Dakota $5.54Notice Indiana. It is the cheapest state for gasoline and nowhere near the cheapest for diesel ($5.85, right on the national average).

That is taxes: Indiana’s diesel and gasoline tax-and-fee stacks are both heavy; gasoline just happens to be oversupplied locally this week. California is #1 in both products because the policy stack and the isolated refining system hit gasoline and diesel.

For truckers, the Labor Day print is not a holiday story. At 6.5 mpg, $5.85 diesel is about 90 cents a mile in fuel alone. At California’s $7.71, it is about $1.19 a mile. That differential moves into grocery shelves, housing materials, and every other good that rides a trailer.

What Energy Policy adds to a gallon of gas

1. The statutory tax line

Federal (both states):

18.4¢/gal gasoline · 24.4¢/gal diesel. Unchanged since 1993.

California (effective July 1, 2026, CDTFA): Gasoline state excise: 63.4¢/gal (up from 61.2¢ on July 1; inflation-indexed under SB 1)

Diesel state excise: 48.2¢/gal (up from 46.6¢)

Sales tax still applies to gasoline at a reduced state rate of 2.25%, plus district add-ons that vary by county. The prepayment rate for gasoline is 8.0¢/gal effective July 1, 2026. Diesel is taxed at a much higher sales-tax rate (prepayment 42.5¢/gal).

Underground storage tank fee: 2.0¢/gal

Combined EIA/Tax Foundation “state taxes and fees” on gasoline: about 73.6¢/gal — highest in the country.

Texas (unchanged since 1991): Gasoline excise: 20.0¢/gal

Diesel excise: 20.0¢/gal

No local motor-fuel excise. No state sales tax on highway gasoline/diesel; the 20-cent motor-fuel tax is the consumption tax. Texas Comptroller: “LOCAL RATE: NONE.”

On statutory excise plus federal alone:

CA gasoline: 18.4 + 63.4 = 81.8¢

TX gasoline: 18.4 + 20.0 = 38.4¢

Statutory gap: 43.4¢/gal before sales tax and climate programs.

2. The programs that do not appear as a “gas tax” on the pump sticker

The California Energy Commission’s own price-breakdown page is blunt about two line items that Texas does not have:

Cap-and-Trade pass-through: about 25¢/gal (CEC, January 2026 estimate, 6% of the then-retail price)

Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) pass-through: about 17¢/gal (CEC, January 2026 estimate, 4%)

Those two programs alone are about 42¢ — more than Texas’s entire state gasoline tax, twice over. They move with allowance and credit markets, so they are not a fixed “tax,” but they are a state-imposed cost that refiners recover at the rack.

Add sales tax on a ~$5.80 gallon (2.25% state plus districts, commonly ~10–18¢ depending on city) and the UST/oil-spill nickels, and credible tallies put California policy adders around $1.20–$1.40 a gallon. Carscoops, citing the July 1, 2026 increase, put the combined state taxes, fees, and mandates at roughly $1.20/gal.

Texas policy adders: 38.4¢.

Policy gap: on the order of $1.00–$1.05/gal.

That still leaves about $1.00–$1.10 of the $2.12 California–Texas retail gap unexplained by the tax-and-program stack.

That remainder is market structure:

CARB gasoline. California requires a unique reformulated blend (CARBOB). It cannot be freely backfilled from Gulf Coast or Midcontinent barrels the way Texas regular can. When a West Coast refinery stumbles, the substitute molecule has to be imported by water.

PADD 5 isolation. There is no large-diameter products pipeline from Gulf Coast megarefineries into California. Washington, Oregon, Nevada, Arizona, and California live inside that isolated system — which is why they cluster at the top of every ranking, not just California.

Refining concentration and higher operating costs. Fewer, more tightly regulated plants, higher land/labor/compliance costs, and thinner spare capacity.

Distribution and retail margin. CEC regularly shows California distribution/marketing margins running richer than the national average.

Alaska and Hawaii are expensive for a simpler reason: they are islands. Their state gasoline taxes are among the lowest in America (Alaska 8.95¢, Hawaii 18.5¢). Geography, not Sacramento, is doing that work. California is the expensive-state problem that is mostly a policy-plus-spec problem.

3. Diesel makes the contrast even sharper

California diesel does not just carry the 48.2¢ state excise. It carries a 13% sales tax concept (prepay 42.5¢ from July 1), cap-and-trade, LCFS, and CARB diesel specs. IFTA’s California combined diesel rate has run near 97.9¢/gal (excise plus the “component b” add-on) for third-quarter 2026 interstate accounting. Texas IFTA diesel is 20¢. A truck crossing from El Paso to San Diego is not paying “a little more.” It is changing tax regimes.

What this weekend actually costs

A family putting 15 gallons in a sedan:Indiana: $51.70

Texas: $55.33

U.S. average: $62.21

California: $87.12

A contractor filling a 30-gallon diesel pickup:Oklahoma: $161.50

Texas: $163.92

U.S. average: $175.50

California: $231.28

IndoAviation Plus – Direktorat Jenderal Perhubungan Udara Kementerian Perhubungan (Kemenhub) memproyeksikan adanya rata-rata kenaikan harga tiket pesawat domestik kelas ekonomi sekitar 8 persen pada September 2026. Kenaikan ini merupakan imbas langsung dari penyesuaian batas maksimal fuel surcharge (biaya tambahan bahan bakar) menjadi 40 persen dari Tarif Batas Atas (TBA).

Direktur Jenderal Perhubungan Udara, Lukman F. Laisa, menegaskan bahwa penyesuaian ini sama sekali bukan bentuk kenaikan tarif dasar (basic fare) penerbangan. Langkah ini murni diambil regulator untuk merespons fluktuasi harga bahan bakar pesawat (avtur) dunia, khususnya di Indonesia, sebagai akibat dinamika global.

“Penyesuaian fuel surcharge murni dilakukan untuk merespons dinamika harga avtur dunia, bukan merupakan kenaikan tarif dasar tiket pesawat. Komponen fuel surcharge juga wajib dicantumkan secara terpisah pada tiket agar masyarakat mendapatkan informasi tarif secara transparan,” ujar Lukman F. Laisa melalui sebuah pernyataan resmi kepada media, Jumat (4/9).

Berdasarkan data publikasi per 1 September 2026, rata-rata harga avtur mengalami eskalasi sekitar 6,5 persen. Harga bahan bakar penerbangan tersebut merangkak naik dari Rp21.892 per liter pada Agustus menjadi Rp23.315 per liter pada September.

Merespons hal tersebut, Kemenhub menerbitkan Keputusan Menteri Perhubungan Nomor KM 1041 Tahun 2026. Melalui regulasi ini, batas maksimal fuel surcharge ditetapkan sebesar 40 persen dari TBA, naik dari batas bulan sebelumnya yang berada di level 30 persen.

Meski batas maksimal dinaikkan, Lukman meluruskan persepsi bahwa hal tersebut tidak otomatis membuat harga tiket melonjak hingga 40 persen.

“Angka 40 persen itu mengacu pada persentase maksimal dari Tarif Batas Atas untuk komponen fuel surcharge, bukan 40 persen dari total harga tiket,” jelasnya.

Ia juga menekankan bahwa maskapai tidak diwajibkan menerapkan batas maksimal tersebut dan dapat menetapkan besaran di bawah 40 persen sesuai efisiensi dan kebijakan operasional masing-masing perusahaan.

Sebagai bentuk perlindungan konsumen, Kemenhub mewajibkan seluruh badan usaha angkutan udara mematuhi ketentuan tarif yang berlaku. Total harga tiket beserta komponen tambahan yang dibayarkan oleh penumpang dilarang keras melampaui Tarif Batas Atas (TBA) yang telah ditetapkan.

Kemenhub menyatakan komitmennya untuk terus menyeimbangkan keberlangsungan operasional maskapai dan daya beli masyarakat. Pengawasan intensif akan terus digulirkan, dan pemerintah siap menjatuhkan sanksi tegas kepada maskapai yang terbukti melakukan pelanggaran tarif.

text:
RRI.CO.ID, Jakarta - Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) is strengthening the ecosystem for sustainable biofuel production by introducing the U‑Collect Box, a technology‑based system designed to collect used cooking oil.

The initiative is supported by environmental, economic, and social studies to ensure a traceable and sustainable supply chain.

“Used cooking oil can gain economic value when collected and reused as an energy source,” said Head of BRIN’s Center for Sustainable Industrial and Manufacturing Systems Research, Nugroho Adi Sasongko, as quoted on BRIN's official website.

He noted its potential to be processed into low‑carbon fuels such as biodiesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

Head of BRIN’s Energy and Manufacturing Research Organization, Cuk Supriyadi Ali Nandar, added that rising demand for biofuels is driving the need for reliable feedstock. “Research must consider environmental impact, economic feasibility, traceability, and social benefits,” he explained.

Deputy for Infrastructure, Research, and Innovation Dadan M. Nurjaman praised the U‑Collect Box for turning waste into valuable resources while reducing pollution.

He encouraged its adoption across BRIN’s science and technology parks, including the B.J. Habibie Technopark in Serpong, which is being developed as an Eco Science Technopark.

The program is supported by PT Noovoleum Indonesia, whose commissioner Sendy Soeriaatmadja said the U‑Collect Box was designed to help households and small businesses collect used oil while promoting circular economy awareness.

Equipped with IoT sensors, apps, and dashboards, the system monitors volumes in real time and ensures traceability.

So far, about 300 units have been deployed in Indonesia and Thailand, collecting 6,000 liters of used oil and producing 5,800 liters of biofuel. Community engagement programs have reached 400 schools, while 55 percent of program revenue is redistributed to local communities.

BRIN is also conducting life cycle assessments to measure greenhouse gas emissions across the supply chain. “Circular value begins when waste is collected. That process must be organized, and every liter recorded,” said researcher Hismiaty Bahua.

She cautioned that emissions could arise at each stage--from collection and transport to processing and distribution--underscoring the need for efficiency.

The collaboration was formalized through a cooperation agreement between BRIN and PT Noovoleum Indonesia, marked by the launch of U‑Collect Box units at BRIN’s Puspiptek housing complex in Serpong on September 3, 2026. ***

text:
Malaysia Bets on Massage to Boost Tourism

Malaysia looks at turning a centuries-old wellness tradition into a tourism product, stepping up efforts to take its distinctive massage style to international travelers, reports Malaysia official news agency Bernama.

Malaysian massage was introduced as an official tourism product by the Tourism, Arts and Culture Ministry in 2017. Now, the country is seeking to give it a higher profile as part of its broader tourism push, including Visit Malaysia 2026.

Unlike the better-known Thai and Balinese massage traditions, Malaysian massage combines techniques and traditions from several of the country’s communities.

The treatment draws on Malay, Chinese and Indian practices, along with techniques associated with Indigenous communities in Sabah and Sarawak. The result is designed to offer travelers more than relaxation, while also providing an introduction to Malaysian cultural heritage.

Selinastein Mohd Rashid, founder of Nur Taj Spa & Beauty, said to Bernama that traditional techniques, equipment and ingredients help bring local culture into the spa experience.

The treatment begins with a foot-soaking ritual inspired by a traditional Malaysian practice of washing the feet after returning home.

The soak uses ingredients including kaffir lime, betel leaves and pandan leaves. The experience then incorporates Qigong breathing, Indian head massage and Malay and Indigenous techniques from Sabah and Sarawak.

The concept is also gaining traction with international visitors. Malaysian massage has attracted clients from markets including South Korea, India and the Maldives, according to Mohd Rashid.

Unlike some modern spa treatments that rely on machines, Malaysian massage remains hands-on. Practitioners must complete six days of training with a ministry-accredited master trainer before receiving certification.

Malaysia is now taking the concept overseas. Demonstrations have been held in major international cities including New York, London, Berlin and Guangzhou.

Working with theMalaysian Spa Association, practitioners outside the country are also being trained, with the goal of getting Malaysian massage onto international spa menus.

The initiative could give Malaysia another way to differentiate its wellness offering as travelers increasingly seek experiences connected to local culture.

National Heritage Department director-general Mohamad Muda Bahadin said Malaysian massage could potentially be considered part of the country’s heritage, although it has not yet been formally gazetted.

He said preserving the skills and knowledge behind the practice and passing them to future generations could help strengthen its role as a national tourism product and turn it into a globally recognizable travel experience.

Jakarta (tutur.co.id)- Ketahanan energi dan transisi menuju energi rendah karbon menjadi dua isu yang diperkenalkan PT Pertamina (Persero) kepada generasi muda dalam gelaran IdeaFest 2026. Melalui forum tersebut, Pertamina memaparkan Dual Growth Strategy sebagai strategi untuk memperkuat bisnis energi yang telah berjalan sekaligus mengembangkan sumber pertumbuhan baru berbasis energi rendah karbon.

Corporate Secretary Pertamina Arya Dwi Paramita mengatakan, generasi muda memiliki peran penting dalam menghadapi tantangan energi Indonesia di masa depan. Hal itu disampaikannya dalam sesi IdeaFest 2026 di Jakarta Convention Center (JCC) Senayan, Jumat (4/9/2026), berdasarkan keterangan tertulis yang diterima redaksi Tutur.

Menurut Arya, salah satu tantangan utama yang dihadapi Indonesia adalah konsumsi energi nasional yang masih melampaui kemampuan produksi dalam negeri. Kondisi tersebut membuat sebagian kebutuhan energi, khususnya minyak dan gas, masih harus dipenuhi melalui impor dari negara lain.

“Sudah lama sekali kita melakukan impor. Artinya, konsumsi kita lebih tinggi daripada produksi nasional. Di situlah kita perlu mendatangkan pasokan migas dari negara lain untuk memenuhi kebutuhan dalam negeri,” ujar Arya.

Untuk menjawab tantangan tersebut, Pertamina menjalankan Dual Growth Strategy melalui dua arah pertumbuhan yang berjalan beriringan. Di satu sisi, perusahaan memperkuat bisnis energi eksisting guna memenuhi kebutuhan masyarakat saat ini. Di sisi lain, Pertamina mengembangkan bisnis rendah karbon dan energi baru terbarukan sebagai bagian dari persiapan menghadapi kebutuhan energi masa depan.

Pengembangan tersebut mencakup sejumlah sumber energi dan teknologi rendah karbon, mulai dari panas bumi dan energi surya hingga Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF). Salah satu inovasi yang dikembangkan adalah pemanfaatan used cooking oil atau minyak jelantah sebagai bahan baku bahan bakar penerbangan yang lebih rendah emisi.

Minyak jelantah yang telah dikumpulkan diolah di Kilang Pertamina Cilacap bersama bahan baku pendukung lainnya untuk menghasilkan SAF. Arya mengatakan pengembangan teknologi tersebut telah melalui proses riset dan pengujian dalam beberapa tahun sebelum digunakan dalam penerbangan.

Menurut Pertamina, pengembangan energi rendah karbon tidak berarti meninggalkan sumber energi yang masih dibutuhkan masyarakat saat ini. Bisnis energi eksisting tetap diperkuat untuk menjaga ketahanan pasokan nasional, sembari perusahaan membangun portofolio energi yang lebih ramah lingkungan dan berkelanjutan.

title: Japan Airlines Invests In Rival Korean Air, Expanded Partnership Coming
description:
Japan Airlines has just acquired a stake in Korean Air’s parent company, Hanjin KAL, and it’s expected to lead to an expanded strategic partnership.
Japan Airlines reveals surprise investment in Korean Air It’s an interesting time for aviation in South Korea, given that Korean Air and Asiana have merged, and the two airlines will shortly be operating under one brand.
But now we can add another airline to the list, as Japan Airlines has also purchased an undisclosed stake in the South Korean flag carrier.
The view is that Japan Airlines is coming in as a white knight for Hanjin KAL Chairman Cho Won-tae, whose control is under threat from the company’s second largest shareholder, Hoban Group.
The thing that many people forget is that even though Korean Air and Japan Airlines are rivals, they have cooperated for decades, specifically in the form of a codeshare agreement between South Korea and Japan.
text:
Japan Airlines has just acquired a stake in Korean Air’s parent company, Hanjin KAL, and it’s expected to lead to an expanded strategic partnership.

This is rather unusual on the surface, since Korean Air is in SkyTeam, and has a joint venture with Delta, while Japan Airlines is in oneworld, and has a joint venture with American. What’s really going on here, and is there an ulterior motive?!

Japan Airlines reveals surprise investment in Korean Air

It’s an interesting time for aviation in South Korea, given that Korean Air and Asiana have merged, and the two airlines will shortly be operating under one brand. Delta has already invested in Korean Air’s parent company, which seems logical enough, given the close commercial cooperation between the airlines.

But now we can add another airline to the list, as Japan Airlines has also purchased an undisclosed stake in the South Korean flag carrier. The view is that Japan Airlines is coming in as a white knight for Hanjin KAL Chairman Cho Won-tae, whose control is under threat from the company’s second largest shareholder, Hoban Group.

More specifically, the company’s second largest shareholder is currently within 1% of having the same size stake as the largest shareholder, and the Korean Development Bank could soon sell its 10%+ stake. So the concern is that a big fight could be triggered between the two largest shareholders, though both Delta and Japan Airlines are expected to side with the Chairman.

The thing that many people forget is that even though Korean Air and Japan Airlines are rivals, they have cooperated for decades, specifically in the form of a codeshare agreement between South Korea and Japan. That’s a high demand market, but there’s also value to coordination there, given limited slots at Tokyo Haneda (HND), plus the overall traffic flow into Tokyo Narita (NRT).

The plan is for the two airlines to work even more closely together, and enter a strategic partnership, which would be a bilateral alliance that goes beyond their participation in their respective global alliances. This will initially include closer cooperation in their core passenger and cargo businesses. The companies will also form a task force to pursue new business opportunities, with options for cooperation with maintenance, sustainable aviation fuel, urban air mobility, and more.

What should we make of this surprise airline investment?

I must say, on the surface this deal strikes me as a bit unusual. This is Japan Airlines’ first investment in a foreign airline, and it’s not like you actually need to invest in an airline in order to cooperate with them. Japanese business culture is also rather transparent and “by the book,” so this isn’t like United CEO Scott Kirby trying to play some sort of strategic game to trick regulators (or… whatever he’s doing, who knows).

Presumably this is a fairly small investment (in terms of percentage ownership), so it’s not like Japan Airlines will get much say in Korean Air’s day-to-day operations. So is Japan Airlines investing in Korean Air because it thinks it’ll get a great direct return on that investment, or is this a situation of helping out Korean Air’s Chairman, and hoping this results in equally favorable treatment in return?

We know that the partnership between Japan and South Korea will be expanded, but what could we realistically see beyond that? I don’t expect we’re going to see anything too radical here:

There’s no way that Korean Air and Japan Airlines would be allowed to join the same transpacific joint venture, so I don’t think this is some grand strategy to get Japan Airlines to leave oneworld and join Korean Air and Delta’s business instead

That being said, I can see how this bilateral agreement could give Japan Airlines an edge over competitor All Nippon Airways in terms of regional service and passenger flows

Belonging to an alliance or joint venture isn’t the same as full-on airline monogamy, so there’s no reason we couldn’t see widespread non-joint venture reciprocity between the airlines when it comes to earning and redeeming points, earning status rewards, etc.

I think the interesting question will be if Delta gets in on this in any way, by association; after all, Delta is soon returning to Tokyo Narita, so could we see something beyond an interline agreement between Delta and Japan Airlines?

Anyway, I’m not expecting anything here that will rock the boat too much, and I suspect this will mostly impact travel between Japan and South Korea. However, who really knows, the airline industry does sometimes throw us curveballs…

Bottom line

Japan Airlines has invested in Korean Air, which is the first foreign airline that the company has taken a stake in. On the surface, it’s odd to see the Japanese oneworld carrier invest in the South Korean SkyTeam carrier, given how they compete. However, the airlines do also cooperate for flights between the two countries. That doesn’t necessarily explain why one needs to take a stake in the other, though.

The airlines claim they’re now working on finding more ways to cooperate, so let’s see how this all evolves…
